desc: COVERAGE is a dataset designed for copy-move forgery detection, containing forged images alongside their original counterparts with similar but genuine objects. It addresses challenges in tamper detection caused by self-similarity in natural images. Each forged-original image pair is annotated with masks indicating duplicated and forged regions, as well as tampering factors or similarity metrics. The dataset supports benchmarking by providing evaluations of forgery quality through both computer vision methods and human detection performance, facilitating research on ambiguity in forgery detection.

Columbia is a dataset designed for image manipulation detection and localization, focusing on identifying and pinpointing forged regions in images such as splicing, copy-move, removal, enhancement, and unknown manipulation types. It supports multi-modal fusion approaches and enables end-to-end detection without requiring preprocessing or postprocessing. The dataset is relevant in digital forensics, addressing challenges posed by manipulated images disseminated through social networks. Models evaluated on Columbia leverage self-supervised learning to detect subtle manipulation traces across diverse forgery types and combinations, with performance assessed through pixel-wise detection and localization accuracy. The dataset emphasizes robustness against common image transformations like resizing and compression, reflecting real-world scenarios. Its inclusion of complex, combined manipulations makes it a challenging benchmark for evaluating the generalization and resilience of image forgery detection systems.

CocoGlide is a dataset designed for image manipulation detection, focusing on identifying tampered regions such as splicing, copy-move, and inpainting. It supports both pixel-level and image-level detection tasks, enabling models to learn features sensitive to manipulation artifacts while maintaining specificity on authentic content. The dataset includes both synthetic and real-world examples, facilitating the development of robust detection systems that generalize across diverse manipulation types. CocoGlide is used to evaluate and train models leveraging multi-view, multi-scale supervision to capture subtle visual cues like noise patterns and boundary artifacts. Its design addresses the challenge of balancing sensitivity to tampering with low false alarm rates on genuine images, making it a key benchmark for image forensics research.

DSO-1 is a dataset designed for image manipulation detection and localization, focusing on identifying tampered regions such as splicing, copy-move, and inpainting. It supports the development and evaluation of deep learning models for forgery detection with high precision, especially in real-world scenarios involving lossy transformations like resizing and compression. The dataset enables pixel-wise detection and localization, making it suitable for both synthetic and real-world image forensics applications. DSO-1 facilitates research on robust and accurate detection of subtle manipulations across diverse image types, supporting advances in attention-based architectures and spatial position encoding to improve localization accuracy.

Casia V1+ is an image dataset designed for forgery classification tasks. It is a modified version of the original Casia V1 dataset, where authentic images overlapping with those in Casia V2 were replaced with images from the COREL dataset to prevent data contamination. This dataset is commonly used to evaluate algorithms for detecting manipulated or forged images, providing a benchmark for image forgery detection research.

SemEval-2010 Task 8 dataset is designed for multi-way classification of semantic relations between pairs of nominals. It contains annotated examples where each pair is labeled with one of several mutually exclusive semantic relation types. The dataset is widely used for relation classification tasks in natural language processing, providing a benchmark for evaluating models that identify and categorize semantic relationships between noun pairs in sentences.

TACRED is a large-scale relation extraction dataset containing over 100,000 examples derived from newswire and web text. It covers 41 relation types used in the TAC Knowledge Base Population challenges, including relations like per:schools_attended and org:members, as well as a no_relation category for unrelated entity pairs. The dataset combines human annotations from TAC KBP challenges with crowdsourced labels, making it a valuable resource for training and evaluating relation extraction models in natural language processing.

FUNSD (Form Understanding in Noisy Scanned Documents) is a dataset consisting of 199 real, fully annotated scanned forms characterized by noise and diverse appearances. It is designed to support multiple document understanding tasks such as text detection, optical character recognition, spatial layout analysis, and entity labeling and linking. The dataset aims to facilitate research in form understanding under challenging conditions typical of scanned documents.

desc: This dataset supports the classification of gene-disease relationship types extracted from biomedical literature. It includes manually annotated sentences and additional sentences generated through a rule-based method with high confidence scores. The dataset is provided in multiple subsets, including a manually annotated set, an unbalanced larger set combining manual and rule-based annotations, and a balanced set ensuring sufficient representation of each relationship class. This resource facilitates research in biomedical relation extraction and knowledge graph construction.

BioRED is a biomedical relation extraction dataset containing multiple entity types such as gene/protein, disease, and chemical, with annotated relation pairs at the document level. It includes around 600 PubMed abstracts and uniquely labels each relation as either a novel finding or previously known background knowledge. This enables automated methods to distinguish between new discoveries and established information in biomedical texts.

Re-TACRED is an enhanced version of the TACRED dataset designed for relation extraction tasks. It improves upon the original by using new crowd-sourced annotations to correct label errors and resolve ambiguities in relation definitions. The dataset contains over 91,000 sentences annotated with 40 different relation types. These improvements result in more accurate and reliable labels, making Re-TACRED a valuable resource for training and evaluating relation extraction models. The dataset was introduced in a paper presented at AAAI 2021.

ChemProt is a dataset comprising PubMed abstracts annotated with chemical-protein interactions by domain experts. It is designed for relation extraction tasks in biomedical text mining and was used in the BioCreative VI shared task to evaluate systems identifying chemical-protein interactions from scientific literature.

MPI-INF-3DHP is a large-scale 3D human pose estimation dataset featuring both indoor and outdoor scenes. It includes recordings of multiple actors performing various activities captured simultaneously from multiple camera views, providing diverse and complex human poses for research in computer vision and pose estimation.

FLoRes-200 is a large-scale multilingual dataset designed for machine translation evaluation, expanding upon FLoRes-101 by covering 200 languages. It includes professional translations in diverse languages, some translated from English and others from Spanish, French, Russian, or Modern Standard Arabic. The dataset addresses challenges related to less standardized languages, requiring specialized translation and verification workflows to ensure quality. FLoRes-200 supports research in low-resource and multilingual machine translation by providing high-quality parallel text across a wide range of languages.

MoNuSeg is a dataset consisting of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained tissue images from multiple patients with tumors across various organs, collected from multiple hospitals. The images are captured at 40x magnification and annotated for nuclei segmentation. Due to the diversity in nuclei appearance and staining protocols, this dataset supports the development of robust and generalizable nuclei segmentation algorithms applicable across different tissue types and clinical settings.

MSMT17 is a large-scale person re-identification dataset featuring multi-scene and multi-time data captured by 15 cameras, including both indoor and outdoor environments. It contains video footage spanning extensive time periods with complex lighting variations, providing diverse conditions for robust person re-identification research. The dataset includes over 4,000 annotated identities and more than 120,000 bounding boxes, making it suitable for training and evaluating person re-identification models under challenging real-world scenarios.

CUHK03 detected is a widely used person re-identification dataset designed for matching individuals across non-overlapping camera views in multi-camera surveillance scenarios. It contains images of pedestrians captured from multiple camera locations with bounding boxes generated by an automatic detector, providing realistic challenges such as occlusions, varying poses, and background clutter. The dataset includes identity annotations that enable evaluation of cross-view matching algorithms. CUHK03 detected is commonly employed to benchmark person re-identification methods, particularly those focusing on appearance-based feature extraction and cross-view retrieval. Standard evaluation metrics such as mean average precision and rank-1 accuracy are used to assess model performance. Its real-world complexity and scale make it a valuable resource for developing robust re-identification models.

CUHK03 Labeled is a person re-identification dataset designed for matching individuals across non-overlapping camera views. It contains approximately 1,400 images of 1,400 pedestrians captured from two distinct camera locations, with each person labeled by identity. The dataset is widely used to evaluate person re-identification algorithms under varying conditions such as lighting, pose, and clothing. Despite its relatively small scale compared to larger benchmarks, it provides valuable challenges including intra-class variation and partial occlusion. Its labeled structure facilitates direct comparison of model performance in identity retrieval tasks, making it suitable for developing and testing re-identification models in controlled environments.

Market-1501 is a large-scale public benchmark dataset for person re-identification. It contains 1,501 identities captured by six different cameras, with over 32,000 pedestrian image bounding boxes detected using a pedestrian detector. Each person has multiple images from different viewpoints. The dataset is divided into training and testing sets, with 750 identities for training and 751 for testing. The official testing protocol includes a probe set of query images used to find correct matches across a large gallery of reference images. Market-1501 is widely used for evaluating person re-identification algorithms in computer vision research.

Occluded-DukeMTMC is a dataset designed for occluded person re-identification tasks. It includes a large number of training images, gallery images, and specifically occluded query images to simulate real-world occlusion challenges. This dataset enables evaluation of person re-identification methods under occlusion conditions without requiring manual cropping or preprocessing steps. It is widely used to benchmark the robustness and effectiveness of algorithms in handling occluded pedestrian images.

The CUHK03 dataset contains over 14,000 images of 1,467 identities captured by six campus cameras, with each identity appearing in images from two different cameras. It provides two types of bounding box annotations: manually labeled and automatically detected. The dataset includes multiple train/test splits, typically with 100 identities reserved for testing and the remainder for training. CUHK03 is widely used for person re-identification research, facilitating evaluation of algorithms under realistic surveillance conditions.

DTU MVS 2014 is a multi-view stereo dataset featuring 80 diverse scenes. Each scene includes 49 or 64 accurately calibrated camera positions and corresponding reference structured light scans, all captured using a 6-axis industrial robot. The dataset offers high-quality data for 3D reconstruction and multi-view stereo research, with a significant increase in scene variety compared to previous datasets.

ActivityNet-1.3 is a large-scale video dataset for temporal action localization, containing over 200,000 video clips annotated with precise start and end times for 200 action categories. It features untrimmed videos from diverse real-world environments, capturing a wide range of human activities with varying durations and overlapping events. The dataset is widely used to evaluate models that detect and localize actions in time, supporting both fully supervised and weakly supervised learning approaches. Performance is typically measured using metrics such as mean average precision and temporal localization accuracy. ActivityNet-1.3's scale, diversity, and detailed temporal annotations make it a benchmark for advancing research in video understanding and action detection.

FineAction contains 103K temporal instances of 106 action categories, annotated in 17K untrimmed videos. It offers new opportunities and challenges for temporal action localization due to its fine-grained action classes, rich diversity, dense annotations of multiple instances, and co-occurring actions of different classes.

The CrossTask dataset consists of instructional videos covering 83 different tasks, each accompanied by an ordered list of manually described steps. It is divided into 18 primary tasks with manually collected videos and temporal step boundary annotations, and 65 related tasks with automatically collected videos lacking annotations. This dataset supports research in video understanding and task recognition by providing detailed procedural information across diverse activities.

Fashion-MNIST is a dataset consisting of 70,000 grayscale images of 28x28 pixels, representing fashion products from 10 categories. It is divided into a training set of 60,000 images and a test set of 10,000 images. The dataset is designed as a direct drop-in replacement for the original MNIST dataset, sharing the same image size, data format, and training/testing split structure. Fashion-MNIST is commonly used for benchmarking machine learning algorithms in image classification tasks involving fashion items.

TACRED is a large-scale relation extraction dataset containing over 100,000 examples derived from newswire and web text. It covers 41 relation types used in the TAC Knowledge Base Population challenges, including relations like per:schools_attended and org:members, as well as a no_relation category for unrelated entity pairs. The dataset combines human annotations from TAC KBP challenges with crowdsourced labels, making it a valuable resource for training and evaluating relation extraction models in natural language processing.

FewRel is a large-scale few-shot relation classification dataset containing 100 relations and approximately 70,000 instances extracted from Wikipedia. It is divided into training, validation, and test sets with distinct relations to evaluate models' ability to generalize to unseen relations. The dataset supports research in few-shot learning and relation extraction tasks.

Social Interaction QA (SIQA) is a question-answering benchmark designed to evaluate social commonsense reasoning. Unlike benchmarks focused on physical or taxonomic knowledge, SIQA emphasizes understanding people's actions and their social implications. It presents questions about everyday social situations, requiring models to infer plausible motivations or consequences behind actions. The dataset includes a diverse set of social scenarios with multiple-choice answers composed of both human-curated and adversarially filtered machine-generated options. SIQA contains over 37,000 question-answer pairs, making it a large-scale resource for assessing models' abilities to reason about social interactions and everyday events.

The Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA) dataset is designed to evaluate commonsense causal reasoning in natural language processing. It contains 1000 multiple-choice questions, divided equally into development and test sets. Each question presents a premise and two alternative sentences, and the task is to select the alternative that is more plausibly causally related to the premise. The correct answer is randomized to ensure a 50% chance baseline for random guessing. COPA is widely used to benchmark models' ability to understand and reason about cause-effect relationships in open-domain contexts.

HotpotQA (BEIR) is a benchmark dataset for evaluating question answering systems, focusing on complex multi-hop questions that require reasoning over multiple documents. It challenges models to retrieve and integrate information from diverse sources to answer fact-based queries accurately. The dataset is commonly used to assess performance on metrics such as exact match and F1 score, emphasizing models' reasoning capabilities and factual correctness. HotpotQA is integrated into the BEIR benchmark to evaluate retrieval effectiveness in knowledge-intensive tasks, making it valuable for developing and testing advanced question answering and information retrieval models.

SQuAD1.1 dev is a benchmark dataset for reading comprehension and question answering tasks, consisting of human-annotated questions derived from Wikipedia articles. Each question is paired with an answer span that appears verbatim in the corresponding passage, enabling evaluation of a model's ability to locate and extract precise answers from natural language text. The dataset is widely used to assess the performance of question-answering systems, with evaluation metrics including exact match and F1 score. It serves as a standard benchmark for evaluating state-of-the-art natural language processing models, particularly those based on pre-trained language models like BERT. Its well-structured format and real-world relevance enable researchers to test and compare models across various downstream tasks, including text retrieval, semantic understanding, and contextual reasoning.

FQuAD is a French reading comprehension dataset consisting of questions and answers based on Wikipedia articles. It includes over 25,000 samples in version 1.0 and more than 60,000 samples in version 1.1, designed to support machine reading comprehension tasks in French.

BLURB (Biomedical Language Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark) is a comprehensive benchmark designed to advance biomedical natural language processing. It consolidates thirteen publicly available datasets spanning six diverse biomedical NLP tasks, including named entity recognition, relation extraction, and question answering. BLURB aims to provide a unified evaluation framework to facilitate the development and comparison of models, particularly leveraging transfer learning from pretrained language models. The benchmark reports macro-averaged scores across tasks to ensure balanced evaluation and includes a model-agnostic leaderboard to track community progress. By offering broad coverage of biomedical NLP challenges, BLURB seeks to accelerate research and improve applications in this critical domain.

The Natural Questions dataset is a large-scale question answering benchmark consisting of real anonymized Google search queries paired with corresponding Wikipedia pages. Each example includes a question, a long answer which is a passage from the Wikipedia page that answers the question, and one or more short answer spans extracted from the long answer. Some examples have no answer, indicated by empty long and short answer annotations. In some cases, the long answer is present but no short answer spans are identified. Additionally, a small portion of examples contain yes/no answers instead of span-based answers. This dataset is widely used for training and evaluating machine reading comprehension and open-domain question answering systems.

PubMedQA is a dataset designed for question answering in the biomedical domain, focusing on answering research questions with yes, no, or maybe responses based on corresponding PubMed abstracts. It contains a small set of expert-labeled questions, a larger set of unlabeled questions, and a substantial number of artificially generated question-answer instances, enabling research in machine reading comprehension and biomedical natural language processing.

Multiple choice question answering dataset based on the United States Medical Licensing Exams (USMLE). It includes professional medical board exam questions in three languages: English, simplified Chinese, and traditional Chinese, with a substantial number of questions for each language.

The Story Cloze dataset is designed to evaluate a model's ability to understand and complete short narrative contexts. It consists of short stories with two sentences followed by two possible endings, where the task is to select the ending that logically and coherently completes the story. This dataset assesses language models' narrative comprehension, reasoning, and contextual inference capabilities. It has been widely used as a benchmark for evaluating models' ability to generate plausible and contextually appropriate continuations, emphasizing understanding of story coherence rather than large-scale data volume. Performance is typically measured using accuracy in selecting the correct ending, highlighting models' strengths and weaknesses in narrative reasoning tasks.

StrategyQA is a question answering benchmark designed to evaluate multi-step implicit reasoning. It contains approximately 2,780 examples, each comprising a strategy question, its decomposition into reasoning steps, and supporting evidence paragraphs. The questions are concise, cover diverse topics, and require inference of underlying strategies to arrive at correct answers.

NQ (BEIR) is a benchmark dataset for knowledge-base question answering, containing natural language questions paired with factual answers derived from curated online knowledge bases. It is designed to evaluate models' ability to retrieve and reason over precise, domain-specific factual information across diverse topics. The dataset reflects real-world query patterns and requires understanding of context and semantic relevance. NQ is commonly used to benchmark question answering systems, assessing exact match and F1 scores, and is employed to evaluate large language models such as T5 and XLNet. It highlights challenges in factual accuracy, contextual understanding, and domain generalization, making it a valuable resource for advancing knowledge-based QA research.

The OBQA dataset is a benchmark for evaluating question-answering models focused on knowledge-based and community-based queries. It contains structured questions and corresponding answers derived from real-world knowledge sources, enabling assessment of a model's ability to retrieve and reason over factual information. The dataset emphasizes accuracy and relevance in open-domain question answering, with performance typically measured using metrics such as exact match and F1 score. OBQA supports evaluation of both traditional and large language models, particularly in few-shot and zero-shot settings where models infer answers without extensive task-specific training. It reflects real-world query patterns and challenges, including ambiguity, context dependency, and factual consistency, making it a critical benchmark for assessing modern language models' capabilities in practical, human-like question answering scenarios.

FiQA-2018 is a question answering dataset included in the Benchmarking Information Retrieval (BEIR) collection, designed to evaluate information retrieval and question answering systems across diverse, real-world domains. It contains factual questions paired with relevant passages, emphasizing domain-specific and community-driven knowledge retrieval. As part of a heterogeneous benchmark, FiQA-2018 supports assessment of various retrieval paradigms, including dense, sparse, and re-ranking methods. The dataset challenges models to retrieve accurate answers from unstructured text, particularly in out-of-distribution scenarios. Its inclusion in BEIR facilitates robust comparisons of retrieval systems under varied task conditions, focusing on generalization and zero-shot performance. Models are typically evaluated using standard metrics such as exact match and F1, balancing computational efficiency and accuracy.

DaNetQA is a question answering dataset for yes/no questions. These questions are naturally occurring ---they are generated in unprompted and unconstrained settings. Each example is a triplet of (question, passage, answer), with the title of the page as optional additional context. The text-pair classification setup is similar to existing natural language inference tasks. By sampling questions from a distribution of information-seeking queries (rather than prompting annotators for text pairs), we observe significantly more challenging examples compared to existing NLI datasets. ### Example ``` { "text": "В период с 1969 по 1972 год по программе «Аполлон» было выполнено 6 полётов с посадкой на Луне. Всего на Луне высаживались 12 астронавтов США. Список космонавтов Список космонавтов — участников орбитальных космических полётов Список астронавтов США — участников орбитальных космических полётов Список космонавтов СССР и России — участников космических полётов Список женщин-космонавтов Список космонавтов, посещавших МКС Энциклопедия астронавтики.", "question": "Был ли человек на луне?", "label": true, "idx": 5 } ``` ### How did we collect data? All text examples were collected in accordance with the methodology for collecting the original dataset. Answers to the questions were received with the help of assessors, and texts were also received automatically using ODQA systems on Wikipedia. Human assessment was carried out on Yandex.Toloka. *Additionally, to increase number of samples and the distribution of yes/no answers, we added extra data in the same format (data were collected from Yandex.Toloka while generating MuSeRC dataset).

**Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs** **DROP** is a crowdsourced, adversarially-created, 96k-question benchmark, in which a system must resolve references in a question, perhaps to multiple input positions, and perform discrete operations over them (such as addition, counting, or sorting). These operations require a much more comprehensive understanding of the content of paragraphs than what was necessary for prior datasets. The questions consist of passages extracted from Wikipedia articles. The dataset is split into a training set of about 77,000 questions, a development set of around 9,500 questions and a hidden test set similar in size to the development set. Source: Image Source:

**BioASQ** is a question answering dataset. Instances in the BioASQ dataset are composed of a question (Q), human-annotated answers (A), and the relevant contexts (C) (also called snippets). Source: Image Source:

**MultiRC** (**Multi-Sentence Reading Comprehension**) is a dataset of short paragraphs and multi-sentence questions, i.e., questions that can be answered by combining information from multiple sentences of the paragraph. The dataset was designed with three key challenges in mind: * The number of correct answer-options for each question is not pre-specified. This removes the over-reliance on answer-options and forces them to decide on the correctness of each candidate answer independently of others. In other words, the task is not to simply identify the best answer-option, but to evaluate the correctness of each answer-option individually. * The correct answer(s) is not required to be a span in the text. * The paragraphs in the dataset have diverse provenance by being extracted from 7 different domains such as news, fiction, historical text etc., and hence are expected to be more diverse in their contents as compared to single-domain datasets. The entire corpus consists of around 10K questions (including about 6K multiple-sentence questions). The 60% of the data is released as training and development data. The rest of the data is saved for evaluation and every few months a new unseen additional data is included for evaluation to prevent unintentional overfitting over time. Source: Image Source:

TrecQA is a question answering dataset derived from the TREC Question Answering tracks spanning 1999 to 2004. It includes two versions: raw and clean. Both share the same training set, but differ in development and test sets. The clean version excludes questions without answers or with only positive/negative labels in development and test sets. It contains over a thousand questions in training and smaller sets for development and testing, along with tens of thousands of question-answer pairs. TrecQA is widely used for evaluating answer selection and retrieval models in natural language processing research.

The StoryCloze dataset is designed to evaluate commonsense story understanding by requiring models to select the correct ending to a four-sentence story. It consists of a large collection of five-sentence everyday stories that capture causal and temporal relationships between events. This dataset supports research in narrative comprehension, script learning, and commonsense reasoning, providing a challenging benchmark for language understanding models.

desc: MedTurkQuAD is a specialized Turkish-language dataset created for question-answering tasks in the medical domain. It contains approximately 8,200 question-answer pairs sourced from Turkish Wikipedia and medical theses from the Council of Higher Education in Turkey, providing domain-specific textual content. The dataset facilitates the development and evaluation of machine learning models aimed at understanding and retrieving precise answers from medical texts in a low-resource language setting. Models trained on MedTurkQuAD are typically evaluated using Exact Match and F1 score metrics. Transformer-based pre-trained language models, such as BERTurk variants, have been successfully fine-tuned on this dataset, demonstrating competitive performance despite the challenges posed by the Turkish language's limited resources and the complexity of medical terminology. MedTurkQuAD serves as an important benchmark for medical question-answering research in Turkish.

The WikiQA corpus is a publicly available dataset designed for open-domain question answering research. It consists of question and sentence pairs derived from Bing query logs to represent real user information needs. Each question is associated with a relevant Wikipedia page, and candidate answer sentences are extracted from the summary section of that page, which typically contains the most important information. The dataset includes thousands of questions and tens of thousands of candidate sentences, with a subset labeled as correct answers. WikiQA facilitates the development and evaluation of question answering systems by providing realistic and challenging data.

BoolQ is a large-scale yes/no question answering dataset consisting of naturally occurring questions paired with corresponding Wikipedia passages. Questions are derived from anonymized Google search queries identified as likely yes/no questions and are verified by human annotators for clarity and answerability. Annotators select relevant passages from Wikipedia articles and label each question with a yes or no answer based on the passage content. The dataset is designed to support research in machine reading comprehension and natural language understanding tasks involving binary question answering.

The **NewsQA** dataset is a crowd-sourced machine reading comprehension dataset of 120,000 question-answer pairs. * Documents are CNN news articles. * Questions are written by human users in natural language. * Answers may be multiword passages of the source text. * Questions may be unanswerable. * NewsQA is collected using a 3-stage, siloed process. * Questioners see only an article’s headline and highlights. * Answerers see the question and the full article, then select an answer passage. * Validators see the article, the question, and a set of answers that they rank. * NewsQA is more natural and more challenging than previous datasets. DROP Test is a benchmark dataset for reading comprehension and discrete reasoning in natural language processing. It contains a large set of adversarially crafted questions derived from paragraphs, requiring models to resolve references across multiple text positions and perform discrete operations such as addition, counting, or sorting. The dataset emphasizes deeper understanding beyond simple fact retrieval, making it more challenging than standard reading comprehension tasks. All questions are in English and crowdsourced to ensure diversity and realism. Models are evaluated using F1 and exact match metrics, with expert human performance significantly outperforming current state-of-the-art systems. DROP Test serves as a critical benchmark for assessing a model's ability to perform complex, real-world reasoning tasks and generalize effectively.

SQuAD1.1 is a widely used benchmark dataset for machine reading comprehension and question answering tasks. It consists of over 100,000 question-answer pairs derived from Wikipedia articles, where each question is associated with a specific answer span within the passage. The dataset is designed to evaluate models' ability to understand context, locate relevant information, and extract precise answers. Questions and answers are in English, and the dataset is commonly used to assess performance on metrics such as exact match (EM) and F1 score. Its scale and real-world relevance make it a standard for training and evaluating models in natural language understanding, including architectures like BERT and T5. The dataset has been instrumental in advancing end-to-end reading comprehension systems, enabling the development of models that can perform contextual reasoning and span prediction. SQuAD2.0 dev is a benchmark dataset for evaluating question answering systems, derived from Wikipedia articles. It contains a large number of human-annotated questions, including both answerable and unanswerable queries, which require models to determine when no answer is supported by the text. This dataset challenges models to perform reading comprehension and precise answer span extraction, promoting robustness and reasoning capabilities. It is widely used to assess natural language processing models using metrics such as exact match and F1 score, making it a standard benchmark for evaluating the performance of pre-trained language models in question answering tasks.

SQuAD2.0 is a large-scale, text-based question answering dataset designed for evaluating natural language understanding and machine reading comprehension. It consists of over 100,000 human-annotated questions and answers derived from Wikipedia, with each question requiring the model to extract precise answers from a given passage. The dataset introduces complex, open-ended questions and includes "unanswerable" entries, which significantly increases the challenge for models by requiring reasoning and uncertainty detection. It is primarily used to assess the performance of language models in tasks such as reading comprehension, information retrieval, and answer generation. Evaluation is typically conducted using metrics like exact match (EM) and F1 score. AI2 Diagrams (AI2D) is a dataset of over 5000 grade school science diagrams with over 150000 rich annotations, their ground truth syntactic parses, and more than 15000 corresponding multiple choice questions. Source: Image Source:

The MSRVTT-QA dataset is a benchmark for video-based Visual Question Answering (VQA) built on the MSR-VTT video dataset. It contains videos paired with natural language questions and corresponding answers, designed to evaluate models' ability to understand and reason about video content. This dataset supports research in video understanding and multimodal reasoning tasks by providing diverse question-answer pairs grounded in real-world video clips.

VCR (Question Answering and Reasoning) is a multimodal visual question answering dataset designed to evaluate models' ability to reason about images and answer complex, context-dependent questions. It combines images with natural language questions and answers, requiring models to understand visual content, perform logical inference, and align textual queries with image semantics. The dataset emphasizes reasoning over simple recognition, featuring questions that demand understanding of spatial relationships, object interactions, and narrative context. While not a pretraining dataset per se, VCR serves as a benchmark for evaluating vision-and-language models, particularly those trained on image-caption data. Models are assessed on their ability to ground language in visual regions without explicit supervision, demonstrating sensitivity to syntactic and semantic relationships between words and image elements. The dataset is used to evaluate the performance of vision-language models such as VisualBERT, which leverages self-attention mechanisms to align text and image regions.

In this project, we introduce InfoSeek, a visual question answering dataset tailored for information-seeking questions that cannot be answered with only common sense knowledge. Using InfoSeek, we analyze various pre-trained visual question answering models and gain insights into their characteristics. Our findings reveal that state-of-the-art pre-trained multi-modal models (e.g., PaLI-X, BLIP2, etc.) face challenges in answering visual information-seeking questions, but fine-tuning on the InfoSeek dataset elicits models to use fine-grained knowledge that was learned during their pre-training.

VQA-X is a multimodal visual question answering dataset designed to evaluate and advance the generation of natural language explanations (NLEs) for image-based reasoning tasks. It consists of image-question-answer triples, with a focus on generating human-interpretable, ground-truth-level explanations that accompany answers to visual questions. The dataset supports multi-task pretraining, enabling models to jointly learn from diverse vision-language tasks such as VQA, e-SNLI-VE, and VCR, thereby improving both answer accuracy and explanation quality. Unlike traditional VQA benchmarks, VQA-X emphasizes the integration of explanation generation with task prediction, promoting a unified, coherent reasoning framework. The dataset challenges models to produce plausible, contextually relevant explanations that are not only accurate but also preferred by human annotators over baseline responses. It consists of image-question-answer triples where questions demand reasoning beyond simple object recognition, such as understanding actions, spatial relationships, and temporal dynamics. The dataset is part of a broader vision-and-language benchmark that emphasizes grounded language understanding through visual context. It is used to assess models' performance in tasks requiring alignment between natural language and visual content, particularly in scenarios involving compositional reasoning and syntactic structure. VCR is often used in pre-training and evaluation of vision-and-language models like VisualBERT, which leverage image-caption data to learn cross-modal representations. A Winograd schema is a pair of sentences that differ in only one or two words and that contain an ambiguity that is resolved in opposite ways in the two sentences and requires the use of world knowledge and reasoning for its resolution. The schema takes its name from a well-known example by Terry Winograd. The set would then be presented as a challenge for AI programs, along the lines of the Turing test. The strengths of the challenge are that it is clear-cut, in that the answer to each schema is a binary choice; vivid, in that it is obvious to non-experts that a program that fails to get the right answers clearly has serious gaps in its understanding; and difficult, in that it is far beyond the current state of the art. ### Task Type Logic and Reasoning, World knowledge. Background: The high volume of research focusing on extracting patient information from electronic health records (EHRs) has led to an increase in the demand for annotated corpora, which are a precious resource for both the development and evaluation of natural language processing (NLP) algorithms. The absence of a multipurpose clinical corpus outside the scope of the English language, especially in Brazilian Portuguese, is glaring and severely impacts scientific progress in the biomedical NLP field. Methods: In this study, a semantically annotated corpus was developed using clinical text from multiple medical specialties, document types, and institutions. In addition, we present, (1) a survey listing common aspects, differences, and lessons learned from previous research, (2) a fine-grained annotation schema that can be replicated to guide other annotation initiatives, (3) a web-based annotation tool focusing on an annotation suggestion feature, and (4) both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation of the annotations. Results: This study resulted in SemClinBr, a corpus that has 1000 clinical notes, labeled with 65,117 entities and 11,263 relations. In addition, both negation cues and medical abbreviation dictionaries were generated from the annotations. The average annotator agreement score varied from 0.71 (applying strict match) to 0.92 (considering a relaxed match) while accepting partial overlaps and hierarchically related semantic types. The extrinsic evaluation, when applying the corpus to two downstream NLP tasks, demonstrated the reliability and usefulness of annotations, with the systems achieving results that were consistent with the agreement scores. Conclusion: The SemClinBr corpus and other resources produced in this work can support clinical NLP studies, providing a common development and evaluation resource for the research community, boosting the utilization of EHRs in both clinical practice and biomedical research. **AmsterTime** dataset offers a collection of 2,500 well-curated images matching the same scene from a street view matched to historical archival image data from Amsterdam city. Unlike existing benchmark datasets, AmsterTime is directly crowdsourced in a GIS navigation platform (Mapillary). In turn, all the matching pairs are verified by a human expert to verify the correct matches and evaluate the human competence in the Visual Place Recognition (VPR) task for further references. The properties of the dataset are summarized as: - 1200+ license-free images from the Amsterdam City Archive, representing urban places in the city of Amsterdam, captured in the past century by many photographers. - All archival queries are matched with street view images from Mapillary. - All matches are verified by architectural historians and Amsterdam inhabitants. - Image pairs are archival and street views capturing the same place with different cameras, time lags, structural changes, occlusion, viewpoint, appearance, and illuminations. - The dataset exhibits a domain shift between query and the gallery due to significant difference between scanned archival and street view images. Two sub-tasks are created on the dataset: - **Verification** is a binary classification (auxiliary) task to detect a pair of archival and street-view images of the same place. The verification task for AmsterTime dataset has all of the crowdsourced image pairs as positive labeled, where the same number of negative samples are generated by randomly pairing archival and street-view images summing up to a total of 2,462 pairs in the verification task. - **Retrieval** is the main task corresponding to VPR, in which a given query image is matched with a set of gallery images. The Balanced Choice of Plausible Alternatives dataset is a benchmark for training machine learning models that are robust to superficial cues/spurious correlations. The dataset extends the COPA dataset(Roemmele et al. 2011) with mirrored instances that mitigate against token-level superficial cues in the original COPA answers. The superficial cues in the original COPA datasets result from an unbalanced token distribution between the correct and the incorrect answer choices, i.e., some tokens appear more in the correct choices than the incorrect ones. Balanced COPA equalizes the token distribution by adding mirrored instances with identical answer choices but different labels. The details about the creation of Balanced COPA and the implementation of the baselines are available in the paper.

**MoleculeNet** is a large scale benchmark for molecular machine learning. Mini-Imagenet 5-way (1-shot) is a widely used benchmark dataset in few-shot learning designed to evaluate meta-learning models' ability to recognize new classes with only one example per class. It contains 100 classes with 100 images each, organized into support and query sets. Each task involves five classes (5-way) with one labeled example per class (1-shot) in the support set, and multiple query images for evaluation. This dataset facilitates rigorous assessment of models' capacity to learn generalizable representations and adapt quickly to unseen classes with minimal labeled data. Its controlled structure and small sample size make it suitable for evaluating data-efficient learning strategies such as learning-to-learn frameworks and hierarchical inference methods.

The STL-10 dataset is an image dataset derived from ImageNet, commonly used to evaluate unsupervised feature learning and self-taught learning algorithms. MultiOFF is a multimodal dataset designed for the classification of offensive content in internet memes, combining both image and text modalities. It addresses the challenge of detecting hate speech, offensive language, and aggression in memes, which often rely on implicit humor, sarcasm, and the interplay between visual and textual elements. The dataset was constructed using memes related to the 2016 U.S. presidential election, reflecting real-world social and political contexts. MultiOFF facilitates research in multimodal offensive content detection by enabling models to jointly analyze images and their accompanying text, overcoming limitations of single-modality approaches. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate that early fusion techniques combining both modalities outperform text-only or image-only baselines in precision, recall, and F-score. This dataset is particularly valuable for advancing understanding and development of classifiers capable of nuanced interpretation of complex, multimodal social media content, contributing to safer and more responsible online communication.

The Actor-Action Dataset (A2D) by Xu et al. [29] serves as the largest video dataset for the general actor and action segmentation task. It contains 3,782 videos from YouTube with pixel-level labeled actors and their actions. The dataset includes eight different actions, while a total of seven actor classes are considered to perform those actions. We follow [29], who split the dataset into 3,036 training videos and 746 testing videos. As we are interested in pixel-level actor and action segmentation from sentences, we augment the videos in A2D with natural language descriptions about what each actor is doing in the videos. Following the guidelines set forth in [12], we ask our annotators for a discriminative referring expression of each actor instance if multiple objects are considered in a video. The annotation process resulted in a total of 6,656 sentences, including 811 different nouns, 225 verbs and 189 adjectives. Our sentences enrich the actor and action pairs from the A2D dataset with finer granularities. For example, the actor adult in A2D may be annotated with man, woman, person and player in our sentences, while action rolling may also refer to flipping, sliding, moving and running when describing different actors in different scenarios. Our sentences contain on average more words than the ReferIt dataset [12] (7.3 vs 4.7), even when we leave out prepositions, articles and linking verbs (4.5 vs 3.6). This makes sense as our sentences contain a variety of verbs while existing referring expression datasets mostly ignore verbs.

Next generation task-oriented dialog systems need to understand conversational contexts with their perceived surroundings, to effectively help users in the real-world multimodal environment. Existing task-oriented dialog datasets aimed towards virtual assistance fall short and do not situate the dialog in the user's multimodal context. To overcome, we present a new dataset for Situated and Interactive Multimodal Conversations, SIMMC 2.0, which includes 11K task-oriented user assistant dialogs (117K utterances) in the shopping domain, grounded in immersive and photo-realistic scenes. The dialogs are collected using a two-phase pipeline: (1) A novel multimodal dialog simulator generates simulated dialog flows, with an emphasis on diversity and richness of interactions, (2) Manual paraphrasing of the generated utterances to collect diverse referring expressions. We provide an in-depth analysis of the collected dataset, and describe in detail the four main benchmark tasks we propose. Our baseline model, powered by the state-of-the-art language model, shows promising results, and highlights new challenges and directions for the community to study.

When glancing at a magazine, or browsing the Internet, we are continuously being exposed to photographs. Despite of this overflow of visual information, humans are extremely good at remembering thousands of pictures along with some of their visual details. But not all images are equal in memory. Some stitch to our minds, and other are forgotten. In this paper we focus on the problem of predicting how memorable an image will be. We show that memorability is a stable property of an image that is shared across different viewers. We introduce a database for which we have measured the probability that each picture will be remembered after a single view. We analyze image features and labels that contribute to making an image memorable, and we train a predictor based on global image descriptors. We find that predicting image memorability is a task that can be addressed with current computer vision techniques. Whereas making memorable images is a challenging task in visualization and photography, this work is a first attempt to quantify this useful quality of images.

TREC-COVID (BEIR) is a heterogeneous benchmark dataset for evaluating biomedical information retrieval systems. It comprises 18 diverse text retrieval datasets spanning multiple domains and tasks, including clinical, scientific, and public health contexts, enabling broad assessment of out-of-distribution generalization. The dataset is designed to evaluate state-of-the-art retrieval models—such as lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, and re-ranking architectures—under realistic and varied conditions. By incorporating diverse query and document pairs, BEIR highlights performance trade-offs between computational efficiency and retrieval accuracy. Results indicate that while BM25 remains a robust baseline, re-ranking and late-interaction models achieve superior zero-shot performance at higher computational cost, whereas dense and sparse methods are more efficient but often underperform. VisDA2017 is a large-scale benchmark dataset for domain adaptation in computer vision, focusing on synthetic-to-real image classification. It contains images from two distinct domains: a synthetic source domain with rendered 3D models and a real-world target domain with natural images, covering 12 object categories. The dataset is designed to evaluate algorithms that address domain shift challenges, where training and testing data distributions differ significantly. VisDA2017 supports unsupervised domain adaptation tasks, emphasizing methods that align feature representations across domains to improve classification accuracy on the target domain. It is widely used to benchmark approaches such as adversarial training and feature alignment techniques under realistic domain adaptation scenarios.

Office-Home is a benchmark dataset designed for domain adaptation tasks, comprising four distinct domains: Art, Clipart, Product, and Real-World. Each domain contains images from 65 categories, including artistic images such as sketches and paintings (Art), clipart images (Clipart), object images without backgrounds (Product), and regular camera-captured images (Real-World). The dataset includes approximately 15,500 images, with an average of around 70 images per category, supporting research in cross-domain visual recognition and adaptation.

Duke to Market is a dataset designed for unsupervised domain adaptation in person re-identification (re-id) within a 3D spatial framework. It extends traditional 2D re-id by incorporating 3D point cloud representations derived from 2D images, capturing both body structure and appearance in a geometrically coherent manner. The dataset enables the evaluation of models that learn pedestrian representations directly from sparse 3D point clouds, leveraging the inherent structure of human bodies to improve robustness against scale, viewpoint, and occlusion variations. Unlike conventional 2D-based approaches, this setup introduces a novel paradigm where 3D geometry provides complementary information to visual appearance, enhancing matching accuracy in real-world scenarios. The dataset supports evaluation under domain shift conditions, where models are trained on labeled source data and tested on unlabeled target domains without requiring explicit annotations. It consists of graph-based inputs derived from Wikipedia knowledge graphs, where each graph encodes semantic relationships between entities and their attributes. It is an essential dataset for researchers and developers working on object detection, segmentation, and pose estimation tasks.

COCO minival is a subset of the Microsoft COCO dataset used for evaluating pose estimation models, particularly in human pose detection. It contains annotated images with keypoint locations for human body parts such as hands, head, and elbows, serving as a standard benchmark for assessing the accuracy and robustness of pose estimation algorithms. The dataset is widely used to compare performance across single-stage and multi-stage methods, with evaluation metrics typically based on mean per-keypoint accuracy (mAP) and precision-recall curves. Given its diverse and real-world imagery, COCO minival presents challenges related to pose variation, occlusion, and scale diversity. LLVIP is a large-scale visible-infrared paired dataset designed for low-light vision tasks. It contains over 30,000 images organized into more than 15,000 paired visible and infrared images captured across various scenes, including dark and daytime environments. The dataset supports multiple research applications such as image-to-image translation between visible and infrared modalities, image fusion, and pedestrian detection under low-light conditions. Additionally, the original unregistered image and video pairs are provided to facilitate diverse computer vision tasks involving cross-modality data.

The **m**inimalist **hist**opathology image analysis dataset (**MHIST**) is a binary classification dataset of 3,152 fixed-size images of colorectal polyps, each with a gold-standard label determined by the majority vote of seven board-certified gastrointestinal pathologists. MHIST also includes each image’s annotator agreement level. As a minimalist dataset, MHIST occupies less than 400 MB of disk space, and a ResNet-18 baseline can be trained to convergence on MHIST in just 6 minutes using approximately 3.5 GB of memory on a NVIDIA RTX 3090. As example use cases, the authors use MHIST to study natural questions that arise in histopathology image classification such as how dataset size, network depth, transfer learning, and high-disagreement examples affect model performance. Each video in this dataset is annotated by multiple free-text descriptions, action labels, action intervals and classes of interacting objects. 267 different users were presented with a sentence, which includes objects and actions from a fixed vocabulary, and they recorded a video acting out the sentence. The dataset is challenging for state-of-the-art models but easy for humans, who achieve over 95% accuracy, making it a benchmark for commonsense reasoning in natural language processing.

**CREMA-D** is an emotional multimodal actor data set of 7,442 original clips from 91 actors. These clips were from 48 male and 43 female actors between the ages of 20 and 74 coming from a variety of races and ethnicities (African America, Asian, Caucasian, Hispanic, and Unspecified). Actors spoke from a selection of 12 sentences. The sentences were presented using one of six different emotions (Anger, Disgust, Fear, Happy, Neutral, and Sad) and four different emotion levels (Low, Medium, High, and Unspecified). Participants rated the emotion and emotion levels based on the combined audiovisual presentation, the video alone, and the audio alone. Due to the large number of ratings needed, this effort was crowd-sourced and a total of 2443 participants each rated 90 unique clips, 30 audio, 30 visual, and 30 audio-visual. 95% of the clips have more than 7 ratings.

OCR is inevitably linked to NLP since its final output is in text. Advances in document intelligence are driving the need for a unified technology that integrates OCR with various NLP tasks, especially semantic parsing. Since OCR and semantic parsing have been studied as separate tasks so far, the datasets for each task on their own are rich, while those for the integrated post-OCR parsing tasks are relatively insufficient. In this study, we publish a consolidated dataset for receipt parsing as the first step towards post-OCR parsing tasks. The dataset consists of thousands of Indonesian receipts, which contains images and box/text annotations for OCR, and multi-level semantic labels for parsing. The proposed dataset can be used to address various OCR and parsing tasks.

The Kleister NDA dataset has 540 Non-disclosure Agreements, with 3,229 unique pages and 2,160 entities to extract.

It comprises approximately 3.02 million sentence pairs, providing extensive bilingual data to support the training and evaluation of translation models between Vietnamese and English. The dataset facilitates advancements in neural machine translation by offering diverse and representative linguistic contexts, enabling models to capture complex syntactic and semantic nuances inherent in both languages. PhoMT has been instrumental in benchmarking state-of-the-art translation systems, including large language models and transformer-based architectures, demonstrating significant improvements in translation quality as measured by standard metrics such as BLEU scores. Math-Vision (Math-V) dataset is a meticulously curated collection of 3,040 high-quality mathematical problems with visual contexts sourced from real math competitions. Spanning 16 distinct mathematical disciplines and graded across 5 levels of difficulty, our dataset provides a comprehensive and diverse set of challenges for evaluating the mathematical reasoning abilities of LMMs. Through extensive experimentation, we unveil a notable performance gap between current LMMs and human performance on Math-Vision, underscoring the imperative for further advancements in LMMs. Moreover, our detailed categorization allows for a thorough error analysis of LMMs, offering valuable insights to guide future research and development.

Recent advances in large language models have led to the development of multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), which take both image data and text as an input. Virtually all of these models have been announced within the past year, leading to a significant need for benchmarks evaluating the abilities of these models to reason truthfully and accurately on a diverse set of tasks. When Google announced Gemini (Gemini Team et al., 2023), they showcased its ability to solve rebuses—wordplay puzzles which involve creatively adding and subtracting letters from words derived from text and images. The diversity of rebuses allows for a broad evaluation of multimodal reasoning capabilities, including image recognition, multi- step reasoning, and understanding the human creator’s intent. We present REBUS: a collection of 333 hand-crafted rebuses spanning 13 diverse cate- gories, including hand-drawn and digital images created by nine contributors. Samples are presented in Table 1. Notably, GPT-4V, the most powerful model we evaluated, answered only 24% of puzzles correctly, highlighting the poor capabilities of MLLMs in new and unex- pected domains to which human reasoning generalizes with comparative ease. Open-source models perform even worse, with a median accuracy below 1%. We notice that models often give faithless explanations, fail to change their minds after an initial approach doesn’t work, and remain highly uncalibrated on their own abilities.

VQA v2 test-dev is a multimodal visual question answering dataset consisting of image-text pairs where images are paired with natural language questions and corresponding answers. Given a text query and list of molecules without any reference textual information (represented, for example, as SMILES strings, graphs, or other equivalent representations) retrieve the molecule corresponding to the query. From a text description of a molecule, the model must incorporate the information in the description into a semantic representation which can be used to directly retrieve the molecule. This requires the integration of two very different types of information: the structured knowledge represented by text and the chemical properties present in molecular graphs. **GPQA** stands for **Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark**. It's a challenging dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and scalable oversight mechanisms. Let me provide more details about it: - **Description**: GPQA consists of **448 multiple-choice questions** meticulously crafted by domain experts in **biology, physics, and chemistry**. These questions are intentionally designed to be **high-quality and extremely difficult**. - **Expert Accuracy**: Even experts who hold or are pursuing **PhDs in the corresponding domains** achieve only **65% accuracy** on these questions (or **74%** when excluding clear mistakes identified in retrospect). - **Google-Proof**: The questions are "Google-proof," meaning that even with **unrestricted access to the web**, highly skilled non-expert validators only reach an accuracy of **34%** despite spending over 30 minutes searching for answers. - **AI Systems Difficulty**: State-of-the-art AI systems, including our strongest **GPT-4 based baseline**, achieve only **39% accuracy** on this challenging dataset. The difficulty of GPQA for both skilled non-experts and cutting-edge AI systems makes it an excellent resource for conducting **realistic scalable oversight experiments**. These experiments aim to explore ways for human experts to reliably obtain truthful information from AI systems that surpass human capabilities¹³. In summary, GPQA serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the robustness and limitations of language models, especially when faced with complex and nuanced questions. Its difficulty level encourages research into effective oversight methods, bridging the gap between AI and human expertise. Custom Bird Dataset is a curated collection of bird images annotated for supervised computer-vision tasks. Speech Commands is a widely used audio dataset designed for training and evaluating keyword spotting systems within the speech recognition domain. It consists of short audio recordings of spoken words, enabling models to recognize and transcribe specific keywords from audio input. The dataset facilitates research on real-time and robust speech recognition by focusing on isolated word detection, which is critical for voice-activated applications and command-driven interfaces. Speech Commands presents challenges such as variations in speaker accents, speaking speed, and background noise, reflecting realistic usage scenarios. Its relatively compact and well-structured format makes it suitable for benchmarking lightweight and efficient models, including convolutional and sequence-based architectures. Due to its emphasis on keyword spotting, it serves as a standard benchmark for assessing model performance in recognizing discrete spoken commands, contributing to advances in low-latency speech recognition and embedded voice-controlled systems.

SUPERB (Speech processing Universal PERformance Benchmark) is a benchmark suite for evaluating the quality and transferability of pre-trained speech representations. It aggregates a diverse set of downstream tasks—such as automatic and phoneme-level recognition, speaker identification/verification, speaker diarization, keyword spotting, query-by-example, and emotion/intent classification—using standardized datasets and evaluation protocols. SUPERB emphasizes frozen upstream features with lightweight task-specific heads to isolate representation quality, enabling fair, reproducible comparisons of self-supervised and supervised speech encoders and guiding development of generalizable speech models.

VoxCeleb is a large-scale audio dataset designed for speaker verification and voice-based identity recognition. It consists of approximately 240,000 hours of spoken audio collected from public videos and online sources, featuring over 100,000 unique speakers. The dataset is divided into two versions: VoxCeleb1 and VoxCeleb2, with VoxCeleb2 offering improved speaker diversity and larger-scale coverage. Each audio clip is associated with speaker identities, enabling supervised learning of voice characteristics for identity verification tasks. Due to its scale and real-world audio conditions, VoxCeleb is widely used to evaluate and train speaker verification models, particularly those leveraging self-supervised learning approaches such as wav2vec 2.0. The dataset presents challenges related to background noise, variable speaking conditions, and speaker variability, making it a key benchmark for assessing robustness and generalization

Apple dataset is a collection of orchard images of apples with corresponding annotations (e.g., bounding boxes, instance masks, and/or count labels) intended for computer vision tasks in agriculture. The dataset serves as a benchmark for developing and evaluating models for automated fruit monitoring and robotic harvesting in practical orchard environments.

arrow is a dataset of arrow symbols collected across diverse scenes and styles, annotated for tasks such as detection, segmentation and orientation estimation. It includes varied arrow shapes, sizes, rotations, occlusions and backgrounds to encourage robustness to visual variability. Designed for training and evaluating models on directional symbol recognition, pose/orientation recovery and scene understanding, arrow is useful for applications in sign interpretation, HCI, robotics and navigation.

The Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech and Song (RAVDESS) contains 7,356 files (total size: 24.8 GB). MAD (Movie Audio Descriptions) is an automatically curated large-scale dataset for the task of natural language grounding in videos or natural language moment retrieval. MAD exploits available audio descriptions of mainstream movies. Such audio descriptions are redacted for visually impaired audiences and are therefore highly descriptive of the visual content being displayed. MAD contains over 384,000 natural language sentences grounded in over 1,200 hours of video, and provides a unique setup for video grounding as the visual stream is truly untrimmed with an average video duration of 110 minutes. 2 orders of magnitude longer than legacy datasets. The dataset supports research on readability assessment, controlled simplification, and downstream tasks (e.g., summarization or question answering) that benefit from more accessible input.

**CREMA-D** is an emotional multimodal actor data set of 7,442 original clips from 91 actors. These clips were from 48 male and 43 female actors between the ages of 20 and 74 coming from a variety of races and ethnicities (African America, Asian, Caucasian, Hispanic, and Unspecified). A curated, balanced test split of the CoughVid crowdsourced cough-audio dataset designed for standardized evaluation of cough-based respiratory classifiers. The split reduces class-imbalance bias for fair comparison of supervised models and is suitable for benchmarking audio classification, cough detection, COVID-19/symptom screening, and robustness analyses.

MAD Dataset is a benchmark collection for anomaly detection that provides labeled normal and anomalous examples across diverse scenes and conditions. It includes multimodal observations (e.g., images with optional depth/thermal or sensor telemetry) and frame- or pixel-level annotations to support detection and localization tasks. Designed to evaluate supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised methods, MAD emphasizes realistic distribution shifts, clutter, and occlusion to benchmark robustness and generalization for industrial inspection, surveillance, and robotic perception.

original_dataset is a benchmark dataset for supervised image restoration that provides high-quality original (clean) images paired with corresponding degraded versions (e.g., motion blur, noise, compression artifacts). Designed to support training and evaluation of denoising, deblurring, and artifact-removal models, it includes diverse scenes, resolutions, and realistic/synthetic degradation types with standardized splits and evaluation protocols to measure restoration quality and generalization.

Common Voice 17.0 (Urdu) is a crowd-sourced corpus of Urdu speech recordings with sentence-level transcriptions and contributor metadata. The dataset supports supervised ASR, speaker recognition, TTS and robustness benchmarking for Urdu-language models.

The dataset is suitable for training and evaluating automatic speech recognition, text-to-speech, and speaker-identification systems, and for benchmarking models on Armenian-language speech under diverse speakers and recording conditions.

MTEB ATEC (default) is a sentence-pair semantic similarity dataset included in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB). MTEB AllegroReviews (default) is a collection of Polish e-commerce product reviews from the Allegro marketplace, including review text and associated metadata such as star ratings and product categories. 8TagsClustering is a clustering benchmark from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) composed of texts annotated with eight distinct topic tags. It is designed to evaluate the ability of text embeddings to separate semantically coherent groups in an unsupervised manner. It serves as a compact, interpretable testbed for developing and benchmarking embedding models for downstream grouping and retrieval tasks.

AmazonCounterfactualClassification (en) is a binary sentiment classification dataset derived from Amazon product reviews that includes original reviews alongside human-created counterfactual variants where minimal edits flip the label. It is designed to evaluate and train models for robust sentiment prediction and to reduce reliance on spurious correlations by testing sensitivity to subtle, causally relevant changes in text. The paired original–counterfactual format supports research in generalization, debiasing, and embedding-based classification methods.

MTEB AmazonCounterfactualClassification (de) is a German-language classification dataset derived from Amazon product reviews, annotated to indicate the presence of counterfactual or hypothetical statements. It pairs short texts with binary labels to evaluate embedding models and classifiers on detecting counterfactual phrasing and subtle semantic shifts in German, enabling benchmarking of semantic understanding, robustness, and downstream performance on counterfactual reasoning tasks.

MTEB AmazonPolarityClassification (default) is a large-scale binary sentiment classification dataset derived from Amazon product reviews. Each example contains review text paired with a polarity label (positive or negative). MTEB AmazonReviewsClassification (en) is an English-language dataset of Amazon product review texts paired with category labels for supervised text classification. The dataset is suited for training and benchmarking embedding-based classifiers, transfer learning, and assessing semantic separability in consumer review domains.

MTEB AmazonReviewsClassification (de) is a German-language dataset of Amazon product reviews paired with class labels for supervised text classification. MTEB AmazonReviewsClassification (es) is a Spanish-language dataset of Amazon product reviews paired with categorical labels for use in text classification benchmarks. MTEB AmazonReviewsClassification (fr) is a French-language dataset of Amazon product reviews paired with product-category labels for supervised multi-class text classification. MTEB AmazonReviewsClassification (zh) is a Chinese-language dataset of Amazon product reviews paired with categorical labels for supervised text classification. Each example contains review text (title and/or body) and an associated label (e.g., product category or star rating), enabling training and evaluation of sentiment/topic classifiers and sentence-embedding models. It serves as a real-world benchmark in MTEB for measuring multilingual embedding quality and classification performance on e-commerce reviews.

MTEB BIOSSES (default) is a biomedical sentence similarity dataset included in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. It is used to evaluate and compare sentence embedding and semantic textual similarity models for domain-specific retrieval, clustering, and downstream biomedical NLP tasks.

MTEB BQ (default) is a dataset within the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) designed to evaluate text embedding models on semantic retrieval and ranking. MTEB Banking77Classification (default) is a classification benchmark based on the Banking77 dataset, containing roughly 13k real-world customer service utterances labeled with 77 fine-grained banking intent categories. MTEB CBD (default) is a curated subset of the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) designed to evaluate sentence- and document-level embedding models across diverse downstream tasks. MTEB CMedQAv1 is a medical question–answer dataset included in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB). MTEB GeoreviewClassification is a text classification dataset of user reviews tied to geographic places, where each review is labeled with the place category (e.g., restaurant, hotel, attraction). It is used in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark to evaluate the quality of sentence embeddings for supervised classification (linear-probe or k-NN) by measuring how well semantic representations separate venue categories. The dataset provides a realistic, domain-specific test of embedding models’ ability to capture fine-grained topical and functional distinctions in short, location-focused text.

GermanSTSBenchmark (default) is a semantic textual similarity dataset within MTEB focused on German. It comprises German sentence pairs annotated with graded similarity scores, providing a standardized benchmark to evaluate sentence and document embeddings on fine-grained semantic equivalence. Commonly used metrics include Spearman/Pearson correlation against human labels; the dataset supports evaluation for tasks such as semantic search, clustering, paraphrase detection, and cross-lingual transfer, helping compare and improve multilingual and German-specific embedding models.

HeadlineClassification (default) is a sentence-level benchmark of news headlines paired with topical labels, designed to evaluate the quality of text embeddings for classification tasks. The dataset tests how well representations capture topical and semantic distinctions by requiring models to assign headlines to discrete categories using simple classifiers (e.g., k-NN or linear probes). It is used in the MTEB suite to compare embedding models on downstream classification performance, robustness to short-text inputs, and generalization across common news topics.

IFlyTek (MTEB default) is a Chinese short-text multi-class classification dataset composed of brief app descriptions or user queries paired with fine-grained category labels. It is designed to evaluate text embedding models on tasks that require distinguishing subtle, domain-specific semantics in very short inputs, such as semantic classification, clustering, and retrieval. The dataset’s many narrow classes and concise texts make it a challenging benchmark for measuring embedding quality and robustness on fine-grained, low-context Chinese language inputs.

MTEB ImdbClassification (default) is a binary sentiment-classification benchmark based on the IMDB movie-review dataset, containing balanced labeled long-form reviews (roughly 25k train / 25k test). It is included in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark to evaluate how well text embeddings capture sentiment and document-level semantics by measuring downstream classification performance using simple classifiers (e.g., linear probes or k-NN). The task is useful for assessing embedding quality for sentiment analysis, transfer learning, and supervised downstream tasks on longer, real-world text.

MTEB InappropriatenessClassification (default) is a classification dataset of short texts annotated for inappropriate content (e.g., offensive, abusive, hateful, or sexual material). Each example pairs a text snippet with labels indicating its appropriateness, enabling evaluation of embedding-based classifiers and downstream moderation systems. It is included in MTEB to benchmark embedding quality on safety-sensitive, semantically nuanced classification tasks.

JDReview is a Chinese product review dataset sourced from JD.com and included in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB). It pairs user-written review texts with associated ratings, making it suitable for embedding-based tasks such as sentiment classification, semantic similarity, clustering, and retrieval in e-commerce contexts. The dataset is commonly used to evaluate how well text embeddings capture sentiment and product-related semantics in Chinese review language, supporting development of recommendation, review-analysis, and semantic-search systems.

KinopoiskClassification is a Russian-language movie review classification dataset sourced from Kinopoisk, containing user reviews paired with rating/sentiment labels.
