tagged_one250v4_wikigold_split is a sense-tagged dataset for word sense disambiguation built from Wikipedia contexts (WikiGold). It contains annotated instances for 250 ambiguous target lemmas (version 4) with standard train/validation/test splits; each example includes the sentence context, target token position, and a gold sense label mapped to a predefined sense inventory. The split is intended for supervised WSD training and evaluation, benchmarking contextualized embeddings, sense induction, and transfer-learning approaches.

tagged_one250v5_wikigold_split is a Wikipedia-derived entity linking / wikification dataset based on the tagged_one250v5 collection, partitioned according to the Wikigold split. Each example pairs text passages with annotated mention spans linked to gold-standard Wikipedia identifiers (and typically includes surface forms and character offsets). The dataset provides train/validation/test folds for supervised training and benchmarking of mention detection, candidate generation, and entity disambiguation models on realistic Wikipedia contexts.

tagged_one250v6_wikigold_split is a token-level labeled dataset derived from Wikipedia text, provided as a split aligned with the WikiGold benchmark. Each example pairs tokenized sentences with sequence labels (e.g., BIO-style entity tags) suitable for supervised sequence-labeling tasks such as named entity recognition or chunking. It is intended for training and evaluating NER/sequence-labeling models and assessing generalization on Wikipedia-style language.

tagged_one250v7_wikigold_split is a small annotated sequence-labeling dataset for named entity recognition using the WikiGold partition. It provides tokenized sentences with token-level entity tags (BIO-style) aligned to Wikipedia-derived entity annotations, packaged into train/validation/test splits following the WikiGold split. Version v7 contains a curated set intended for low-resource evaluation and fine-tuning experiments, making it suitable for benchmarking NER models, few-shot learning, and domain-adaptation studies. Data is typically formatted as token-per-line with sentence boundaries and corresponding tags.

tagged_one250v8_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated dataset for named entity recognition and mention detection derived from Wikipedia and aligned with the WikiGold evaluation split. It provides tokenized sentences with gold entity tags (BIO-style) and document identifiers, organized into train/validation/test partitions. The dataset is intended for supervised training and benchmarking of sequence-labeling and entity-linking models, and for evaluating model generalization on Wikipedia-style text and mention-boundary recovery.

tagged_one250v9_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from Wikipedia text with manual linguistic annotations and a standardized WikiGold train/dev/test split. Each example contains tokenized sentences with corresponding tag sequences (e.g., named-entity, POS, or chunk labels depending on the annotation layer), sentence boundaries, and document identifiers. Provided as version v9 across ~250 source documents, the dataset is intended for training and evaluating supervised sequence-tagging models, benchmarking generalization to Wikipedia-style text, and experiments in domain adaptation and transfer learning.

tagged_one500v0_wikigold_split is an English token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from the WikiGold annotations. It contains Wikipedia sentences with manually annotated named-entity tags in BIO format and uses the standard WikiGold train/validation/test split. The dataset is intended for supervised NER and sequence-labeling experiments, evaluation of model generalization on Wikipedia-style text, and transfer/fine-tuning studies.

tagged_one500v1_wikigold_split is a split of the WikiGold corpus prepared for sequence labeling and entity recognition. It provides sentence-tokenized text with manually annotated named-entity mentions and their types, organized into predefined training, validation and test subsets. The collection is suitable for supervised NER training, mention-detection evaluation, and entity-linking experiments on Wikipedia-style text, enabling reproducible benchmarking of tagging models and transfer studies.

tagged_one500v2_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated dataset combining the tagged_one500v2 resource with the WikiGold split of Wikipedia text, formatted for sequence-labeling tasks. It provides sentences with token annotations (e.g., named-entity and/or part-of-speech tags) and standard train/validation/test splits, enabling supervised training and evaluation of token classification models. The dataset is suited for benchmarking NER/POS systems, studying domain transfer on encyclopedic text, and comparing sequence-labeling architectures.

tagged_one500v3_wikigold_split is a compact, gold-standard dataset of ~500 Wikipedia-derived passages token-tagged for entity mentions and linked to canonical Wiki entries. Version v3 provides span-level annotations (entity boundaries and types) along with resolved wiki identifiers, and comes pre-partitioned into train/validation/test splits following the WikiGold protocol. It is intended for supervised sequence labeling and entity linking research, enabling benchmarking of NER models, mention detection, and mention-to-Wikipedia disambiguation on high-quality, real-world text.

tagged_one500v4_wikigold_split is a small-scale English sequence-labeling benchmark derived from the WikiGold corpus, providing token-level and span-level entity annotations with a predefined train/validation/test split. It is intended for supervised named entity recognition and information-extraction experiments, facilitating model development, evaluation, and comparison on high-quality Wikipedia-based entity annotations. The split supports reproducible training and validation for tasks such as sequence tagging, span classification, and transfer/fine-tuning studies.

tagged_one500v5_wikigold_split is a Wikipedia-derived corpus with manually annotated keyphrases arranged according to the WikiGold train/validation/test split. Each instance pairs article text with token- or phrase-level tags marking gold keyphrases, enabling supervised training and evaluation of keyphrase extraction, sequence tagging, and candidate ranking models. The standardized split supports reproducible benchmarking of extraction methods on a Wikipedia-based gold standard.

tagged_one500v6_wikigold_split is a token-level dataset for supervised named entity recognition (NER) created by aligning the Tagged One500 v6 corpus to the WikiGold annotation standard. It provides tokenized sentences paired with BIO-style entity tags (e.g., PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) organized into standard train/validation/test splits. The split is intended for training and benchmarking sequence-labeling models and for evaluating model generalization under a Wikipedia-derived gold annotation scheme. Data is suitable for experiments in NER, entity linking pretraining, and cross-dataset evaluation.

tagged_one500v7_wikigold_split is a token-level labeled split of the WikiGold keyphrase dataset (500 Wikipedia articles) formatted for sequence labeling. Each document is tokenized and annotated with BIO-style tags marking gold keyphrases; the release includes reproducible train/validation/test splits and metadata. It is intended for supervised keyphrase extraction and sequence-labeling research (e.g., CRF, BiLSTM-CRF, Transformer token classifiers) and for evaluation with standard precision/recall/F1 metrics on encyclopedic text. Version v7 reflects specific preprocessing and tokenization choices.

tagged_one500v8_wikigold_split is a token-level labeled dataset for named entity recognition derived from the WikiGold corpus. It contains Wikipedia-style sentences annotated with IOB entity tags (common types such as PER, LOC, ORG, MISC) and is provided with standard training, validation, and test splits following the WikiGold partitioning. The dataset is intended for supervised sequence-labeling tasks and benchmarking NER models on encyclopedic text, supporting evaluation of entity detection, classification, and model generalization.

tagged_one500v9_wikigold_split is a Wikipedia-based keyphrase extraction dataset: it pairs article text with token-level BIO/IOB2 span annotations aligned to the WikiGold gold-standard keyphrase lists. This v9 one500 variant provides standardized train/validation/test splits and per-example fields for raw text, tokenization, and per-token labels, enabling supervised sequence-labeling experiments. It is intended for benchmarking and training keyphrase/phrase-detection and span-extraction models, with common evaluation metrics such as precision/recall/F1 at the span level.

tagged_uni50v0_wikigold_split is a mention-level entity linking dataset derived from the WikiGold annotations. It provides textual contexts with tagged mention spans and gold-standard Wikipedia entity identifiers, organized into predefined train/validation/test splits. The collection is intended for training and evaluating entity linking, named-entity disambiguation, and candidate-ranking models, supporting supervised learning and standardized benchmarking of disambiguation accuracy in realistic Wikipedia contexts.

tagged_uni50v1_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated release of the WikiGold corpus prepared for supervised sequence-labeling research. It pairs Wikipedia-derived sentences with a unified tagset for sequence tasks (e.g., NER/POS-style labels) and provides a standardized v1 train/validation/test split for reproducible benchmarking. The dataset is suitable for training and evaluating named-entity recognition, POS tagging, and other sequence-labeling models on encyclopedic text.

tagged_uni50v2_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling dataset built from Wikipedia text using the WikiGold train/dev/test split and the tagged_uni50v2 annotation set. It provides sentences with aligned tokens and linguistic/entity tags in a standard sequence format, suitable for supervised training and evaluation of NER, POS, and other token-classification models. The split enables reproducible benchmarking of sequence-tagging performance and transfer learning across models and tag schemas.

tagged_uni50v3_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from the WikiGold corpus, formatted with a unified 50-label tagset (v3) and provided as standardized train/validation/test splits. Each example contains tokenized Wikipedia sentences paired with BIO-style labels for fine-grained named-entity and entity-type classification. The split facilitates supervised training and evaluation of sequence tagging models and benchmarking of NER and fine-grained entity classification performance on web-domain text.

tagged_uni50v4_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from the WikiGold Wikipedia corpus, with tokens annotated using the "uni50 v4" universal tagset. The collection is provided with standard train/validation/test splits and is intended for supervised tasks such as part-of-speech tagging and named-entity recognition. Annotations preserve WikiGold’s human-labeled entity and syntactic information in encyclopedic text, making the set useful for benchmarking sequence-labeling models, evaluating generalization to Wikipedia-style language, and studying domain-adaptation for taggers and NER systems.

tagged_uni50v5_wikigold_split is a Wikipedia-derived corpus of token-level annotated text prepared from the tagged_uni50 v5 release and partitioned using the WikiGold gold-standard split. Sentences are annotated with mention boundaries and named-entity labels (and optionally entity links), enabling supervised training and evaluation of NER and entity-linking models. The split provides consistent train/validation/test folds for benchmarking, making it useful for model development, cross-dataset validation, and studies of generalization on Wikipedia-style text.

tagged_uni50v6_wikigold_split is a curated text dataset combining token-level annotations on a 50-label universal tagset (v6) with gold-standard Wikipedia entity links derived from the WikiGold corpus. Provided with predefined train/validation/test splits, it supports supervised learning and evaluation for sequence-tagging, named entity recognition, and entity linking/wikification tasks. The dataset enables joint experiments on detecting entity spans, assigning coarse-grained semantic tags, and disambiguating mentions to canonical Wikipedia entries.

tagged_uni50v7_wikigold_split is a curated split of the WikiGold entity-annotated corpus, providing token-level tags, mention spans, and canonical Wikipedia identifiers. Formatted for supervised training and evaluation, it includes predefined train/validation/test splits and a consistent tag schema to support named entity recognition, mention detection, and entity linking tasks. The dataset contains contextual sentences with normalized entity labels, enabling benchmarking of sequence-tagging and linking models and assessment of generalization to Wikipedia-based canonicalization.

tagged_uni50v8_wikigold_split is a labeled keyphrase extraction dataset derived from the WikiGold corpus. It provides Wikipedia articles tokenized and annotated with gold keyphrase labels at the token/phrase level, includes a standardized unigram-based feature representation (uni50v8), and comes with predefined train/validation/test splits. The dataset is intended for supervised sequence-labeling or candidate-ranking experiments, enabling reproducible training and evaluation of keyphrase extraction, phrase spotting, and related information-retrieval models on a curated Wikipedia benchmark.

tagged_uni50v9_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from WikiGold (Wikipedia) that uses the Universal 50-tag schema (v9). Sentences are tokenized and annotated with gold-standard part-of-speech tags and named-entity labels and provided with a standardized train/validation/test split following the WikiGold partition. It is intended for training and benchmarking POS-tagging, NER, and general sequence-labeling models, supporting reproducible evaluation, domain-relevant error analysis, and transfer-learning experiments on Wikipedia-style text.

tagged_uni100v0_wikigold_split is a token-level labeled dataset derived from the WikiGold corpus using the uni100v0 tagging scheme and provided with predefined train/validation/test splits. It contains Wikipedia sentences annotated with gold-standard tags for sequence labeling tasks (e.g., POS tagging or named-entity labeling depending on the tagset), enabling supervised training and evaluation of taggers and sequence models. The split supports benchmarking model accuracy, robustness, and cross-domain transfer on Wikipedia-style text.

tagged_uni100v1_wikigold_split is a token-level BIO-tagged dataset produced by aligning the Uni100 v1 corpus with the WikiGold gold-standard entity annotations and partitioning the data into standard train/validation/test splits. It is designed for supervised named-entity recognition and sequence-labeling experiments on Wikipedia-derived text, enabling model development, evaluation, and transfer-learning comparisons. Each instance provides tokenized text paired with entity labels in a consistent split format suitable for benchmarking NER systems.

tagged_uni100v2_wikigold_split is a labeled dataset for keyphrase extraction and tagging built from Wikipedia text. Each example pairs a document with gold keyphrase annotations and token-level tags, organized according to the WikiGold evaluation split. It is intended for training and evaluating supervised sequence-labeling and keyphrase-generation models, supporting standard extraction metrics (precision/recall/F1) and transfer evaluation against the WikiGold benchmark.

tagged_uni100v3_wikigold_split is a supervised dataset for keyphrase extraction and sequence labeling that pairs tokenized Uni100 v3 documents with WikiGold keyphrase annotations and a standard train/validation/test split. Each example contains document text, token-level annotations (BIO-style keyphrase tags and optional POS/tags), and gold keyphrase spans derived from the WikiGold 100-article set. The split is suitable for training and evaluating sequence-labeling models and keyphrase ranking systems using common metrics (precision/recall/F1), and for research in information extraction, summarization, and downstream retrieval tasks.

tagged_uni100v4_wikigold_split is a token-level, gold-labeled subset of the Uni100 v4 corpus aligned with WikiGold annotations, providing Wikipedia text annotated with entity tags (commonly in BIO/IOB format) and a fixed train/validation/test split. It is designed for supervised sequence-labeling tasks such as named entity recognition and entity linking, enabling standardized evaluation and benchmarking of NER models on Wikipedia-style content.

tagged_uni100v5_wikigold_split is a multilingual, token-level tagged corpus derived from the Uni100 v5 collection with the WikiGold split of gold-standard annotations. It provides sentence-aligned token labels (POS and morphological features, and NER where available), language identifiers, and standardized train/dev/test splits. Designed for benchmarking sequence-labeling tasks (POS tagging, NER, morphological analysis), it supports evaluation of model accuracy and cross-lingual generalization across diverse languages.

tagged_uni100v6_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated corpus derived from the Uni100v6 collection with an evaluation split aligned to the WikiGold benchmark. Each example pairs text tokens or mention spans with gold-standard Wikipedia sense/entity labels, making it suitable for supervised word-sense disambiguation and entity linking. The dataset provides a standardized training/evaluation split to train contextual disambiguation models and compare performance against WikiGold baselines.

tagged_uni100v7_wikigold_split is a multilingual tagged corpus (Uni100 v7) covering ~100 languages, annotated with Universal Dependencies part-of-speech tags and morphological features and partitioned according to a Wikigold-derived train/dev/test split. It provides token-level labels for supervised sequence-labeling tasks (POS and morphological tagging), enabling consistent cross-lingual training, transfer-learning experiments, and benchmarking of multilingual taggers on a standardized evaluation split.

tagged_uni100v8_wikigold_split is a Wikipedia-derived corpus of texts with token- and span-level entity annotations aligned to WikiGold canonical identifiers, provided following the WikiGold train/validation/test split. The dataset contains tagged mentions (e.g., BIO or span labels) and corresponding Wikipedia entity links, making it suitable for named entity recognition, mention detection, and entity linking/disambiguation tasks. It is intended for supervised training and standardized benchmarking of models that map textual mentions to Wikipedia entities and evaluate generalization on WikiGold-style annotations.

tagged_uni100v9_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated split of the WikiGold corpus using the Uni100 v9 universal tagging scheme. It provides sentences from Wikipedia with per-token labels and standard train/validation/test splits for supervised sequence-labeling tasks (e.g., POS tagging and NER). The dataset is intended for training and evaluating sequence tagging models and for benchmarking tagger performance on encyclopedic text using a consistent universal tagset.

tagged_uni250v0_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence‑tagging dataset of Wiki-derived sentences annotated with the Universal POS tagset (versioned as uni250v0) and partitioned using the Wikigold train/validation/test split. It provides standardized tokenization and universal part‑of‑speech labels to support supervised training and evaluation of POS taggers and other sequence‑labeling models, enabling reproducible benchmarking and cross‑domain or transfer experiments on wiki text.

tagged_uni250v1_wikigold_split is a token-level dataset derived from the WikiGold corpus, providing gold-standard entity mention annotations (BIO-style tags) with corresponding Wikipedia link targets and standardized train/validation/test splits. It is intended for training and evaluating named entity recognition, mention detection, and entity linking models on a manually curated Wikipedia-based benchmark.

tagged_uni250v2_wikigold_split is a multilingual token-level tagging benchmark derived from the Tagged_Uni250 v2 corpus with an evaluation split aligned to the WikiGold test set. It contains Wikipedia-derived sentences across 250 languages annotated with universal part-of-speech tags and morphological features, provided in standard token-per-line sentence splits (train/dev/test). The dataset is designed for supervised sequence-labeling tasks such as POS tagging and morphological analysis, and to support multilingual benchmarking, cross-lingual transfer experiments, and low-resource adaptation for models operating on Wikipedia-style text.

tagged_uni250v3_wikigold_split is a token-level labeled corpus combining the Uni250v3 tagged data with the WikiGold NER gold standard and provided as train/validation/test splits. It supplies word tokens paired with named-entity annotations derived from Wikipedia text, enabling supervised training and evaluation of sequence-labeling models for named entity recognition and related tasks. The split facilitates benchmarking, cross-domain evaluation and transfer-learning experiments on Wikipedia-style content.

tagged_uni250v4_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from the WikiGold corpus, provided as a v4 tagged split with annotations mapped to a Universal tagset. It supplies gold-standard tokenization and label sequences suitable for supervised training and evaluation of POS tagging, named-entity recognition, and other sequence-labeling models. The dataset includes predefined train/validation/test partitions for reproducible benchmarking on Wikipedia-derived text and is useful for evaluating model generalization and transfer in encyclopedia-style language.

tagged_uni250v5_wikigold_split is a token-level labeled dataset derived from the WikiGold corpus, providing sentences tokenized and annotated with Universal POS (uni) tags in a standardized train/validation/test split. It is intended for supervised part-of-speech tagging and sequence-labeling research on Wikipedia-style text, enabling consistent benchmarking and comparison of taggers and sequence models. The dataset supplies raw tokens paired with gold universal tag labels, making it suitable for training, evaluation, error analysis, and domain-adaptation experiments.

tagged_uni250v6_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated dataset derived from the WikiGold corpus, preprocessed with the "uni250v6" tagging scheme and provided with standard train/validation/test splits. Each example contains tokenized Wikipedia sentences with per-token labels (entity/mention tags) and minimal metadata. The split is intended for training and evaluating sequence-labeling models (e.g., NER, POS tagging, chunking) and for benchmarking model performance on Wikipedia-style text.

tagged_uni250v7_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated corpus derived from the tagged_uni250v7 collection with a reserved WikiGold split for evaluation. It provides sentences with aligned linguistic tags (e.g., part-of-speech and named-entity labels) organized into train/validation/test partitions, where the WikiGold portion serves as an out-of-domain test set. The dataset is intended for supervised sequence-labeling research — evaluating model training, transfer learning, and generalization to Wikipedia-style text. It is useful for benchmarking POS tagging, NER, and related token classification models.

tagged_uni250v8_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated corpus derived from a WikiGold split and processed under the uni250v8 preprocessing/versioning. Each sentence is segmented and tokens are paired with gold sequence-label annotations (using a unified/universal tagset), and the data is provided in standard train/validation/test splits. It is intended for supervised training and evaluation of sequence-labeling models (e.g., POS/morphological tagging), benchmarking generalization on Wikipedia-style text, and domain-adaptation experiments.

tagged_uni250v9_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence labeling dataset of Wikipedia-derived sentences annotated with Universal POS tags (version 9) and provided in a standard train/validation/test split following the WikiGold partitioning. It is designed for benchmarking POS tagging and related sequence-labeling tasks on Wikipedia-style text, supporting supervised training, cross-domain evaluation, and transfer learning experiments. The dataset includes tokenized sentences and gold-standard tag labels compatible with universal tagsets.

tagged_uni500v0_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from the WikiGold split, with tokens annotated using the uni500v0 universal tagset. It provides gold-standard labeled sequences for training and evaluating sequence-tagging models (e.g., POS tagging and named entity recognition). The split is prearranged for reproducible supervised learning and benchmarking of token-classification architectures and transfer-learning experiments.

tagged_uni500v1_wikigold_split is a token-level named‑entity recognition benchmark derived from the WikiGold corpus, providing BIO-style entity annotations (e.g., PER, LOC, ORG, MISC) with a predetermined train/validation/test split. It is a compact, labeled dataset intended for supervised sequence-labeling, model evaluation, transfer learning and error analysis on Wikipedia-derived text.

tagged_uni500v2_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling benchmark created by re-annotating the WikiGold Wikipedia corpus with the uni500v2 tagset and providing standard train/validation/test splits. Each example is a tokenized sentence from Wikipedia paired with uni500v2 labels (POS/NER-compatible tag inventory) aligned to original tokens. The dataset is designed for training and evaluating supervised sequence-labeling models (POS tagging, NER, joint tagging), transfer learning, and cross-domain robustness experiments.

tagged_uni500v4_wikigold_split is a token-level sequence-labeling benchmark that combines the tagged_uni500v4 corpus with the WikiGold annotation split. It provides sentence-aligned Wikipedia text with tokenized annotations for tasks such as named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging, formatted for supervised training and evaluation with standard train/validation/test splits. The dataset is useful for developing and evaluating sequence-labeling models and studying model generalization on wiki-style text.

tagged_uni500v5_wikigold_split is a preprocessed, token-level labeled split of the WikiGold corpus using the "uni500v5" tagging scheme. It provides sentence-aligned tokens with corresponding labels and standard train/validation/test splits for supervised sequence-labeling tasks (e.g., named entity recognition and entity linking). The dataset is designed for benchmarking and developing models that extract and classify entities from Wikipedia-derived text, supporting evaluation of model accuracy and generalization on encyclopedic content.

tagged_uni500v6_wikigold_split is a Wikipedia-derived dataset of ~500 documents annotated with mention spans and linked Wikipedia entity IDs, organized according to the WikiGold split for evaluation. It provides token-level annotations, canonical entity identifiers (including NIL cases), and predefined train/validation/test partitions. The corpus is intended for supervised learning and benchmarking of mention detection, entity linking/disambiguation, and related information extraction models, with realistic ambiguous mentions and contextual cues for disambiguation.

tagged_uni500v7_wikigold_split is a token-level, gold-annotated subset of the WikiGold corpus prepared with a standard train/validation/test split. Sentences are tokenized and labeled using a universal tagset, making the collection suitable for supervised sequence-labeling tasks (e.g., POS tagging, NER, and related token classification problems). The split enables reproducible benchmarking of sequence models on Wikipedia-style text and comparison of architectures under consistent data partitions.

A token-level sequence-labeling dataset derived from Wikipedia, providing roughly 500 sentences annotated with linguistic tags (compatible with the Universal tagset v8) and partitioned using the WikiGold train/dev/test split. It is intended for training and evaluating POS tagging and named-entity recognition models in low-resource or cross-domain settings, offering tokenized text with gold labels and standardized splits for reproducible benchmarking.

tagged_uni500v9_wikigold_split is a token-level annotated corpus derived from Wikipedia text, formatted with universal part-of-speech tags and sequence-label annotations. It follows the WikiGold train/dev/test split to support supervised training and evaluation of POS tagging and sequence-labeling models. The dataset is useful for benchmarking model performance on encyclopedic language, domain adaptation experiments, and error analysis of token-level classifiers.

mit_restaurants is a curated dataset of real-world restaurant images intended for visual recognition research in dining environments. Images are annotated for tasks such as scene classification, object/dish detection, and fine-grained menu-item recognition under typical restaurant conditions (varying lighting, occlusion, viewpoints, and clutter). The dataset supports training and evaluation of classification, detection, segmentation, and OCR models aimed at applications like food recognition, menu understanding, table-layout analysis, and end-to-end restaurant scene understanding.

data_cartas_layoutv3 is a layout dataset of card-like documents (e.g., business/greeting/postcards) designed for document-layout understanding. It provides images with element-level annotations such as bounding boxes and class labels for common components (titles, logos, body text, images, QR/barcodes) and optional segmentation masks and text transcriptions. The collection spans diverse designs, languages, backgrounds and degradations to support robust training and evaluation of layout parsing, object detection, OCR, template extraction and layout-conditioned generation models.

data_cedulas_layoutv3 is a dataset for document-layout analysis and structured information extraction focused on cédula-style identity documents. It contains photographed and scanned ID card images annotated with layout elements (e.g., portrait, name, ID number, signature, address) as bounding boxes and label metadata, supporting object-detection, segmentation, OCR and key-value pairing tasks. Version 3 improves annotation granularity and robustness to real-world variations (lighting, skew, occlusion, backgrounds), making it suitable for training and evaluating end-to-end pipelines for field localization, automated data capture, and privacy-preserving redaction. Use requires appropriate handling of sensitive personal data and compliance with legal/privacy regulations.

dataset_node: CoNLL03 w. document context␟Named Entity Recognition
desc: CoNLL03 with document context is an augmented version of the CoNLL-2003 NER benchmark that preserves document boundaries and supplies surrounding sentences as context for each annotated sentence. It provides token-level BIO labels for four entity types (PER, LOC, ORG, MISC) on the standard train/dev/test splits (originally in English and German). The dataset supports sentence- and document-level named entity recognition, contextualized sequence labeling, and research into leveraging cross-sentence information or document-level constraints to disambiguate and improve entity predictions.

Privy is a dataset for image privacy research containing real-world images annotated for privacy-sensitive content (e.g., people, faces, personal items and scene regions) with labels and region masks plus optional anonymized variants. It is designed to support supervised training and evaluation of models for privacy attribute recognition, sensitive-region segmentation, and automated anonymization or obfuscation methods. Privy enables benchmarking trade-offs between visual utility and privacy protection across diverse environments and use cases.

Private is a controlled-access dataset of real-world, sensitive data paired with annotations and metadata for supervised ML development and evaluation. It is intended for tasks such as classification, detection, or prediction depending on the contained modalities, and is curated to support realistic training, validation, and robustness testing under practical domain conditions. Access and use are restricted by data-use agreements and privacy-preserving requirements; researchers must follow the dataset’s licensing, security, and ethical guidelines when handling the data.

Szeged_NER is a Hungarian named‑entity recognition corpus containing token‑level annotations for common entity types (e.g., PERSON, LOCATION, ORGANIZATION, MISC). Derived from Hungarian text sources and manually labeled with an IOB/BIO-style scheme, it is intended for training and evaluating sequence‑labeling models for NER in Hungarian. The dataset provides realistic, language‑specific examples useful for benchmarking cross‑lingual and monolingual NER systems and for studying morphology‑rich language challenges in entity recognition.

hausa_voa_ner is a Hausa-language named entity recognition dataset derived from Voice of America news text, with token-level annotations for common entity classes (e.g., PERSON, LOCATION, ORGANIZATION, MISC). It is intended for training and evaluating supervised NER models and for research on NLP for low-resource African languages, supporting monolingual and cross-lingual transfer experiments. The dataset provides sentence-aligned, annotated examples suitable for standard sequence-labeling benchmarks.

job-titles is a corpus of job title strings collected from job postings, resumes, and corporate directories, intended for natural language processing tasks such as title normalization, occupation classification, entity linking, and taxonomy mapping. Entries consist primarily of raw job-title text and frequently include auxiliary metadata (e.g., company, industry, location, or standardized occupational codes) when available, supporting supervised and unsupervised modeling for resume parsing, job recommendation, labor market analysis, and HR automation.

Substance_quantity is an annotated dataset of text examples linking substance mentions to their associated quantity expressions. Each instance pairs named substances (chemicals or ingredients) with normalized quantity values and units, enabling supervised training and evaluation of named-entity recognition, relation extraction, and quantity normalization models. It is intended for automating extraction of formulation data from protocols, safety data sheets, and recipes, and for downstream tasks such as unit conversion, schema population, and question answering about quantities.

Babelscape/multinerd (modified version) is a multilingual named-entity dataset derived from Babelscape resources that provides token-level entity annotations across multiple languages aligned to a shared knowledge base. The modified release contains cleaned annotations, a standardized label ontology and consistent train/validation/test splits to reduce noise and improve comparability. It is suitable for supervised sequence-labeling (NER), cross-lingual transfer, and experiments that combine entity recognition with grounding to a knowledge graph (e.g., BabelNet/Wikidata), serving as a benchmark for multilingual NER, entity linking, and domain adaptation.

hipe2020 is a benchmark dataset released for the HIPE 2020 shared task, focused on automatic processing of historical documents. It contains digitized historical page images paired with human transcriptions and structural annotations (e.g., layout zones, region labels, and entity tags) to facilitate supervised learning for OCR, layout analysis, and information extraction. The dataset captures real-world historical challenges—degraded print, variable typography, and nonstandard language—making it suitable for training and evaluating document understanding and named-entity recognition systems on archival materials.

transformer_dataset_ner is a token-level named entity recognition dataset formatted for training and evaluating transformer-based sequence-labeling models. It provides tokenized sentences with corresponding span-level labels (e.g., BIO/BILOU) and entity-type annotations, together with standard train/validation/test splits. The dataset is suitable for fine-tuning pretrained transformers and benchmarking NER performance using precision, recall, and F1 metrics, and supports typical preprocessing pipelines (subword token alignment, label mapping) used in modern sequence-tagging workflows.

transformer_dataset_ner_kaggle is a token-level named entity recognition dataset curated from a Kaggle source and preformatted for transformer-based models. It contains sentences with aligned token-level labels (commonly BIO) covering standard entity types (e.g., PER, ORG, LOC, MISC), and is provided with train/validation/test splits. The dataset is designed to simplify fine-tuning of BERT/RoBERTa-style architectures by including tokenization-friendly annotations and typical preprocessing notes for label alignment. It is suited for benchmarking token-classification performance (precision/recall/F1) and experimenting with sequence-labeling strategies using transformer encoders.

uner_chn_gsd is a Chinese named‑entity recognition (NER) dataset derived from the Universal Dependencies Chinese-GSD treebank. It provides tokenized Chinese sentences with aligned entity labels suitable for supervised sequence‑labeling, enabling training and evaluation of NER models on Chinese text. The dataset is useful for experiments in word- vs. character-level modeling, cross-domain and cross-lingual transfer, and downstream tasks that require reliable entity extraction in Chinese.

uner_chn_gsdsimp is a Simplified Chinese named-entity recognition (NER) dataset derived from the Universal Dependencies GSD treebank. tico19-test is the official test split of the TICO-19 benchmark, a multimodal dataset of social media posts (images, associated text and metadata) collected during the COVID-19 pandemic. It contains curated, annotated examples for tasks such as content classification, misinformation detection, and image–text relevance, enabling standardized evaluation of models on COVID-related claim detection and multimodal understanding. The split provides ground-truth labels and evaluation protocol for benchmarking model performance and generalization.

FLoRes-200 is a large-scale multilingual dataset designed for machine translation evaluation, expanding upon FLoRes-101 by covering 200 languages. It includes professional translations in diverse languages, some translated from English and others from Spanish, French, Russian, or Modern Standard Arabic. The dataset addresses challenges related to less standardized languages, requiring specialized translation and verification workflows to ensure quality. FLoRes-200 supports research in low-resource and multilingual machine translation by providing high-quality parallel text across a wide range of languages.

Itihasa Dataset is a curated corpus of digitized South Asian historical and epic texts with aligned annotations to support historical document understanding and multilingual NLP. It combines scanned manuscript images and printed pages with transcriptions, token- and sentence-level labels (e.g., named entities, dates, relations), and provenance metadata (language, script, approximate date). Designed as a benchmark with standardized splits and evaluation protocols, Itihasa enables research in OCR/transcription, named-entity and relation extraction, temporal reasoning, and model development for low-resource and ancient-script settings.

WMT14 is a widely used machine translation benchmark from the 2014 Workshop on Machine Translation, providing parallel corpora (commonly English–German and English–French) drawn from news and web sources. It includes standard training data and held-out dev/test splits (e.g., newstest2013/newstest2014) for consistent evaluation. WMT14 is used to train and compare statistical and neural MT systems, typically evaluated with metrics such as BLEU.

UCF Crime Dataset (Subset) is a curated subset of the UCF Crime surveillance video benchmark for video anomaly detection. It contains real-world CCTV-style videos with annotated anomalous events (and accompanying normal footage), including temporal boundaries for abnormal segments across several crime categories. The subset is intended for training and evaluating models on anomaly detection, temporal localization, and weakly-/fully-supervised learning under realistic surveillance conditions with varied viewpoints, lighting, and occlusions.

FaceForensics++ & CelebDFv2 is a combined benchmark for facial forgery and deepfake detection, aggregating large-scale manipulated video datasets with original ground-truth videos. FaceForensics++ provides multiple manipulation types (e.g., DeepFakes, FaceSwap, Face2Face, NeuralTextures) across compression levels, while Celeb-DF v2 supplies more realistic, higher-quality synthesized videos to reduce artifact biases. Together they offer diverse, challenging examples for training and evaluating detection, classification, localization, and robustness of forgery-detection models under varying quality and synthesis methods.

The UCF101 dataset is a large-scale video action recognition dataset consisting of 13,320 video clips categorized into 101 action classes. These classes are grouped into five types: body motion, human-human interactions, human-object interactions, playing musical instruments, and sports. The videos are collected from YouTube, have a fixed frame rate of 25 frames per second, and a resolution of 320 by 240 pixels. The total duration of all videos exceeds 27 hours, making it suitable for training and evaluating machine learning models in video classification and action recognition tasks.

UCF Crime is a large-scale benchmark for anomaly detection and temporal localization in surveillance video. It contains ~1,900 long, untrimmed real-world surveillance clips covering multiple crime/anomaly categories alongside normal activities, with weak video-level labels for training and temporally localized ground-truth annotations for testing. Designed to support weakly supervised and multiple-instance learning approaches, the dataset poses challenges from diverse scenes, long-range temporal context, viewpoint variation and occlusion, enabling evaluation of models for detection and localization of real-world anomalous events.

NSR-VTT is a large-scale video–language benchmark of short web videos paired with human-written captions (≈10k videos, ≈200k captions). It covers diverse scenes and activities across many categories and is widely used for supervised video captioning, video-to-text retrieval, cross-modal representation learning, and multimodal pretraining. NSR-VTT enables evaluation of models’ ability to capture temporal dynamics, actions, and visual context in open-domain videos and supports development of retrieval, grounding, and generation methods for video-language tasks.

**VATEX** is multilingual, large, linguistically complex, and diverse dataset in terms of both video and natural language descriptions. It has two tasks for video-and-language research: (1) Multilingual Video Captioning, aimed at describing a video in various languages with a compact unified captioning model, and (2) Video-guided Machine Translation, to translate a source language description into the target language using the video information as additional spatiotemporal context. Source: Image Source:

The **ActivityNet** dataset contains 200 different types of activities and a total of 849 hours of videos collected from YouTube. ActivityNet is the largest benchmark for temporal activity detection to date in terms of both the number of activity categories and number of videos, making the task particularly challenging. Version 1.3 of the dataset contains 19994 untrimmed videos in total and is divided into three disjoint subsets, training, validation, and testing by a ratio of 2:1:1. On average, each activity category has 137 untrimmed videos. Each video on average has 1.41 activities which are annotated with temporal boundaries. The ground-truth annotations of test videos are not public. Source:

The **Microsoft Research Video Description Corpus** (**MSVD**) dataset consists of about 120K sentences collected during the summer of 2010. Workers on Mechanical Turk were paid to watch a short video snippet and then summarize the action in a single sentence. The result is a set of roughly parallel descriptions of more than 2,000 video snippets. Because the workers were urged to complete the task in the language of their choice, both paraphrase and bilingual alternations are captured in the data. Source: Image Source:

MSR-VTT (Microsoft Research Video to Text) is a large-scale dataset designed for open-domain video captioning. It contains 10,000 video clips spanning 20 categories, each annotated with 20 English sentences collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk. The dataset includes a diverse vocabulary with approximately 29,000 unique words. Standard splits divide the data into training, validation, and testing sets, facilitating consistent evaluation of video captioning models.

iVQA is an open-ended video question answering benchmark designed to provide robust evaluation by including multiple correct answer annotations per question. It contains a large collection of video clips, each paired with a question and several corresponding answers. The dataset is carefully curated to minimize language bias by excluding questions that can be answered without viewing the video content, ensuring that models must analyze the video to respond accurately. This makes iVQA suitable for developing and evaluating video understanding and question answering systems.

The **GQA** dataset is a large-scale visual question answering dataset with real images from the Visual Genome dataset and balanced question-answer pairs. Each training and validation image is also associated with scene graph annotations describing the classes and attributes of those objects in the scene, and their pairwise relations. Along with the images and question-answer pairs, the GQA dataset provides two types of pre-extracted visual features for each image – convolutional grid features of size 7×7×2048 extracted from a ResNet-101 network trained on ImageNet, and object detection features of size Ndet×2048 (where Ndet is the number of detected objects in each image with a maximum of 100 per image) from a Faster R-CNN detector. Source: Image Source:

The **VizWiz**-VQA dataset originates from a natural visual question answering setting where blind people each took an image and recorded a spoken question about it, together with 10 crowdsourced answers per visual question. The proposed challenge addresses the following two tasks for this dataset: predict the answer to a visual question and (2) predict whether a visual question cannot be answered. Source: Image Source:

The MMLU-Pro dataset is an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark. It's designed to be more robust and challenging, aiming to rigorously benchmark large language models' capabilities in language comprehension and reasoning across diverse domains. Here are some key features of the MMLU-Pro dataset: - **Increased Complexity**: It includes more reasoning-focused questions and expands the choice set from four to ten options, reducing the likelihood of random guessing and increasing the evaluation's complexity¹. - **Elimination of Trivial Questions**: MMLU-Pro removes trivial and noisy questions found in the original MMLU, making it a more discriminative benchmark². - **Stability Under Varying Prompts**: The dataset shows greater stability under varying prompts, with a decreased sensitivity of model scores to prompt variations². - **Better Performance with Reasoning**: Models utilizing Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning achieved better performance on MMLU-Pro compared to direct answering². - **Size and Scope**: The dataset contains 12K complex questions across various disciplines¹⁴. **GPQA** stands for **Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark**. It's a challenging dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and scalable oversight mechanisms. Let me provide more details about it: - **Description**: GPQA consists of **448 multiple-choice questions** meticulously crafted by domain experts in **biology, physics, and chemistry**. These questions are intentionally designed to be **high-quality and extremely difficult**. - **Expert Accuracy**: Even experts who hold or are pursuing **PhDs in the corresponding domains** achieve only **65% accuracy** on these questions (or **74%** when excluding clear mistakes identified in retrospect). - **Google-Proof**: The questions are "Google-proof," meaning that even with **unrestricted access to the web**, highly skilled non-expert validators only reach an accuracy of **34%** despite spending over 30 minutes searching for answers. - **AI Systems Difficulty**: State-of-the-art AI systems, including our strongest **GPT-4 based baseline**, achieve only **39% accuracy** on this challenging dataset. The difficulty of GPQA for both skilled non-experts and cutting-edge AI systems makes it an excellent resource for conducting **realistic scalable oversight experiments**. These experiments aim to explore ways for human experts to reliably obtain truthful information from AI systems that surpass human capabilities¹³. In summary, GPQA serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the robustness and limitations of language models, especially when faced with complex and nuanced questions. Its difficulty level encourages research into effective oversight methods, bridging the gap between AI and human expertise. Covering genres such as newswire, broadcast, conversations, weblogs and more in English, Chinese, and Arabic, it provides unified annotations that support training and standardized evaluation of coreference resolution, NER, parsing, semantic role labeling, and joint/multi-task NLP models.

google/xtreme is a multilingual evaluation benchmark that aggregates multiple cross-lingual tasks across 40 languages. It includes sentence-level classification, question answering, token-level labeling, and retrieval/bitext mining tasks to measure zero-shot and few-shot transfer of multilingual encoders. Designed to standardize comparisons of pretrained models (e.g., mBERT, XLM-R), xtreme enables research on cross-lingual representation learning, generalization across languages, and multilingual model robustness.

UNKNOWN is a benchmark dataset for open-set and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection that contains labeled in-distribution classes alongside held-out unknown classes to evaluate models’ ability to recognize unfamiliar inputs. It provides training/validation/test splits with class labels for known examples and a separate pool of unknown-class images used only at evaluation, enabling assessment of detection metrics (AUROC, FPR@95, precision-recall, open-set accuracy). UNKNOWN supports multiple modalities (images and metadata) and diverse domains to stress-test confidence calibration, novelty detection, and open-set classification methods, making it useful for research in robust recognition, anomaly detection, and safe deployment of ML systems.

mit_restaurant is a dataset of restaurant interior images annotated for visual scene understanding. Images are labeled with object-level annotations (e.g., tables, chairs, dishes, people, menus) and scene-layout cues to support tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and spatial layout estimation in dining environments. It is intended for training and evaluating computer vision models for robotics, service automation, and perception systems operating in restaurant-like settings.

germa_ner is a German-language named entity recognition dataset containing tokenized sentences annotated with BIO-style entity labels (commonly including person, location, organization, and miscellaneous). It provides standard train/validation/test splits for supervised sequence-labeling experiments, enabling training and evaluation of NER models, transfer learning, and downstream tasks like entity linking and information extraction on German text.

bigbio/quaero is a biomedical NLP dataset adapted to the BigBio schema from the Quaero corpus. It contains clinical and biomedical text documents with span-level entity annotations (e.g., diseases, chemicals, genes and other biomedical concepts) and associated metadata, prepared for supervised information extraction. The dataset is intended for training and evaluating named entity recognition, entity normalization and related biomedical IE models, supporting reproducible benchmarking within the BigBio ecosystem.

SourceData is a curated multimodal dataset of original (source) media paired with processed or altered variants and rich metadata. It contains diverse, real-world content (images, audio, and text) alongside their unmodified originals and documented transformations (compression, resizing, filtering, editing). Designed for training and benchmarking models for source attribution, provenance analysis, forgery/manipulation detection, and restoration, SourceData supports supervised, contrastive, and domain-adaptation tasks that require recovering, identifying, or reasoning about the true origin of data.

Rodrigo1771/cantemist-ner is a Spanish clinical named-entity recognition dataset from the CANTEMIST initiative, containing clinical case texts annotated with cancer-related entity spans (e.g., tumor mentions, morphology, anatomical sites). Annotations are provided at the token/span level with entity labels suitable for supervised sequence-labeling. The dataset is intended for training and evaluating NER models in the biomedical/clinical domain, supporting research in clinical information extraction, entity normalization, and domain adaptation for Spanish-language medical text.

Acronym Identification is a labeled corpus for detecting acronyms in text and linking them to their long-form expansions. Each example contains contextual sentences or document passages with annotated acronym spans and corresponding full forms (when available), enabling supervised learning for span detection, expansion extraction, and disambiguation. The dataset captures ambiguous acronyms across varied domains and contexts, supporting evaluation of models for abbreviation resolution, named-entity-style identification, and downstream information-extraction tasks in scientific, biomedical, and technical texts.

BioNLP2004 is a curated biomedical text corpus from the BioNLP 2004 workshop containing sentences and abstracts annotated with domain-specific entities (e.g., genes/proteins) and their relationships/interactions. It is designed for supervised training and evaluation of biomedical information extraction tasks such as named entity recognition, relation and interaction extraction, and event detection. The dataset enables development and benchmarking of NLP models that must handle specialized vocabulary, complex syntactic constructs, and domain-specific annotation schemes common in biomedical literature.

Norne is a manually annotated Norwegian named entity recognition dataset containing token-level span annotations for entities in Norwegian text (including Bokmål and Nynorsk). It labels common entity types such as persons, locations, organizations and other domain-relevant classes, and is provided to train and evaluate supervised NER models for Norwegian. The dataset is suitable for benchmarking sequence labeling systems and research on NER in morphologically rich, low-resource languages.

news-test2008 is a standard WMT evaluation set consisting of newswire sentences from 2008 paired with human reference translations for common MT language pairs (e.g., English↔German, English↔French). It serves as a held-out test set for benchmarking machine translation systems, enabling standardized evaluation with metrics like BLEU and chrF. The dataset reflects the formal news domain and is used to assess model generalization and translation quality on contemporary news-style text rather than for model training.

FLORES is a multilingual machine translation benchmark released by Facebook AI Research (notably FLORES-101) that provides curated, human-translated parallel sentences across a large set of languages—including many low-resource and typologically diverse languages. Its sentence-level dev and test splits (drawn and cleaned from sources like Wikipedia) are designed for robust evaluation of neural MT and cross-lingual models across many language pairs. FLORES is widely used to compare translation quality and generalization in multilingual systems and to drive research on low-resource and massively multilingual translation.

UCF-101 is a widely used video dataset for action recognition, containing 13,320 video clips of 101 distinct human actions, each captured from diverse real-world scenarios. The videos are short, typically lasting a few seconds, and are annotated with clear labels that define the action being performed. Despite its relatively small scale compared to modern benchmarks, UCF-101 has served as a foundational resource for training and evaluating action recognition models, particularly in the context of self-supervised and federated learning. Its real-world nature and well-defined action categories make it valuable for assessing model generalization and temporal dynamics in video data. The dataset is often used to benchmark performance on downstream tasks such as video classification, retrieval, and action prediction. GRIND is a benchmark designed to evaluate the adaptive reasoning and generalization ability of large language models under distributional shifts and subtle problem reformulations. Rather than focusing on memorized problem templates or static question-answer patterns, GRIND emphasizes a model’s capacity to adjust its reasoning strategy when familiar problems are modified, extended, or placed in novel contexts. The benchmark typically consists of reasoning tasks in which core logical structures are preserved while surface forms, constraints, or contextual assumptions are altered, requiring the model to demonstrate genuine understanding rather than pattern recall. The problems in GRIND often span logical reasoning, symbolic manipulation, conditional inference, and multi-step decision-making, with a strong emphasis on robustness to prompt variation and perturbation. By introducing small but meaningful changes to otherwise well-known reasoning tasks, GRIND exposes brittleness in models that rely on shallow heuristics or overfitted reasoning shortcuts. As a result, it is particularly effective at distinguishing models that appear strong on conventional reasoning benchmarks from those that can truly generalize their reasoning processes.

AIME 2024 is a multi-institutional, multi-task imaging benchmark designed to accelerate development and evaluation of clinical AI. It provides diverse, de-identified image data across modalities (CT, MRI, ultrasound, and paired photographic images) with structured annotations including pixel-level segmentations, lesion bounding boxes, diagnostic labels, and limited outcome metadata. The dataset includes standardized training/validation/test splits and baseline evaluation scripts for segmentation, classification, detection, and prognosis tasks to support reproducible comparison of models. AIME 2024 targets robustness and generalization research by aggregating data from multiple scanners/sites and by enabling experiments in domain adaptation, semi-supervised learning, and clinically meaningful performance assessment.

**GPQA** stands for **Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark**. It's a challenging dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and scalable oversight mechanisms. Let me provide more details about it: - **Description**: GPQA consists of **448 multiple-choice questions** meticulously crafted by domain experts in **biology, physics, and chemistry**. These questions are intentionally designed to be **high-quality and extremely difficult**. - **Expert Accuracy**: Even experts who hold or are pursuing **PhDs in the corresponding domains** achieve only **65% accuracy** on these questions (or **74%** when excluding clear mistakes identified in retrospect). - **Google-Proof**: The questions are "Google-proof," meaning that even with **unrestricted access to the web**, highly skilled non-expert validators only reach an accuracy of **34%** despite spending over 30 minutes searching for answers. - **AI Systems Difficulty**: State-of-the-art AI systems, including our strongest **GPT-4 based baseline**, achieve only **39% accuracy** on this challenging dataset. The difficulty of GPQA for both skilled non-experts and cutting-edge AI systems makes it an excellent resource for conducting **realistic scalable oversight experiments**. These experiments aim to explore ways for human experts to reliably obtain truthful information from AI systems that surpass human capabilities¹³. In summary, GPQA serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the robustness and limitations of language models, especially when faced with complex and nuanced questions. Its difficulty level encourages research into effective oversight methods, bridging the gap between AI and human expertise. SWE-bench is a benchmark dataset designed to evaluate large language models on real-world software engineering tasks, focusing on their ability to understand, modify, and repair production-level codebases. The dataset is constructed from real GitHub issues collected across a diverse set of open-source repositories. Each instance typically includes a problem description, the corresponding codebase, and a set of automated tests used to verify whether the proposed solution correctly resolves the issue. Unlike synthetic programming benchmarks that test isolated algorithmic skills, SWE-bench emphasizes end-to-end software development capabilities, including code comprehension, debugging, multi-file editing, and adherence to project-specific constraints. Models are required to generate code patches that are not only syntactically correct but also functionally valid, as correctness is determined by whether the patched code passes the repository’s test suite in a controlled execution environment. This execution-based evaluation makes SWE-bench a particularly rigorous and realistic measure of practical coding ability.

MATH 500 is a mathematics reasoning benchmark containing challenging problem-solving tasks that require multi-step derivations. It measures symbolic reasoning quality, accuracy, and consistency on high-difficulty math questions.

The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) is a benchmark designed to evaluate the tool-use and function-calling capabilities of large language models in structured and execution-oriented environments. The benchmark focuses on whether a model can correctly select appropriate functions, generate valid function calls, and populate parameters accurately based on natural language instructions. It is particularly relevant for assessing models intended for agentic systems, API-driven workflows, and tool-augmented reasoning pipelines. BFCL includes a wide range of function-calling scenarios, covering simple single-function invocations as well as more complex cases involving nested calls, parallel tool usage, multi-step planning, and large function libraries. Tasks are designed to stress-test a model’s ability to map unstructured user intent to precise, machine-interpretable actions, while maintaining consistency with function schemas and argument constraints. Correctness is typically evaluated by the executability and semantic validity of the generated calls, rather than by free-form textual similarity.

Aider Polyglot is a multilingual code-generation and code-editing benchmark designed to evaluate large language models across a broad spectrum of programming languages and software development scenarios. The benchmark is built on a curated subset of high-quality programming exercises, primarily sourced from the Exercism platform, and spans multiple languages including Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, C++, and Rust. This diversity enables systematic assessment of cross-language generalization and coding competence. The benchmark emphasizes not only initial code generation but also iterative problem-solving and debugging. Many tasks require the model to refine its solution based on failing test cases or feedback, mirroring realistic developer workflows in which code is incrementally improved rather than written correctly on the first attempt. This iterative structure makes Aider Polyglot particularly effective at evaluating a model’s ability to reason about program behavior, understand error signals, and apply targeted fixes across different programming paradigms.

The MMLU-Pro dataset is an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark. It's designed to be more robust and challenging, aiming to rigorously benchmark large language models' capabilities in language comprehension and reasoning across diverse domains. Here are some key features of the MMLU-Pro dataset: - **Increased Complexity**: It includes more reasoning-focused questions and expands the choice set from four to ten options, reducing the likelihood of random guessing and increasing the evaluation's complexity¹. - **Elimination of Trivial Questions**: MMLU-Pro removes trivial and noisy questions found in the original MMLU, making it a more discriminative benchmark². - **Stability Under Varying Prompts**: The dataset shows greater stability under varying prompts, with a decreased sensitivity of model scores to prompt variations². - **Better Performance with Reasoning**: Models utilizing Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning achieved better performance on MMLU-Pro compared to direct answering². - **Size and Scope**: The dataset contains 12K complex questions across various disciplines¹⁴. 40+ Audio Datasets (1M+ samples) is an aggregated collection of over 40 publicly available audio corpora totaling more than one million audio samples. The collection spans speech (ASR, speaker ID, keyword spotting), music (genre/instrument tagging), environmental and urban sounds, and labeled sound events, with variable durations, sampling rates, languages, and annotation granularities. It’s intended for large-scale supervised and self‑supervised training, transfer learning, and benchmarking of audio classification, recognition, separation, and representation-learning models, providing broad acoustic diversity and real-world recording conditions to evaluate model generalization and robustness.

Common Voice 20 Armenian is a crowd-sourced Armenian speech dataset of short audio clips paired with text transcripts, collected through the Mozilla Common Voice project. It contains recordings from many speakers with metadata (age, gender, accent, client ID) and validation status, providing diversity in voices, recording devices, and acoustic conditions. The dataset is intended for training and evaluating automatic speech recognition, speaker adaptation, language modeling, and related speech technologies, offering a real-world benchmark for supervised speech systems and robustness to heterogeneous recording environments.

Common Voice 17.0 is a large, multilingual, crowd-sourced speech dataset of short voice recordings paired with text transcriptions. It contains validated and unvalidated speech segments contributed by volunteer speakers across many languages, along with optional speaker metadata (age, gender, accent/locale) and quality annotations. Designed for training and evaluating ASR, TTS, voice-activity detection, and speaker or accent studies, it offers diverse accents, recording conditions, and prompts and is distributed under an open license for broad research and development use.

razhan/DOLMA-speech hawrami is a speech dataset of the Hawrami (a Gorani/Kurdish) language containing recorded audio clips paired with orthographic transcriptions and accompanying metadata. Intended for low-resource speech research, it supports development and evaluation of automatic speech recognition, speech-to-text, and speech synthesis systems as well as language documentation and preservation. The dataset provides realistic speaker and recording variability to facilitate robust model training, transfer learning, and experiments in under-resourced language technologies.

Common Voice 11.0 is a large, community-contributed multilingual speech corpus of short audio clips paired with text transcriptions and speaker metadata (age, gender, accent, locale). It contains validated and unvalidated recordings across many languages, along with per-clip validation status and prompts, and is released under an open license for research and commercial use. The dataset is intended for training and evaluating automatic speech recognition, language identification, text-to-speech, and other speech technologies, and supports work on both high-resource and low-resource languages.

Gentlemen is a curated image dataset of male portraits and full‑body photos with diverse ages, ethnicities, poses, lighting, and attire, annotated for tasks such as identity, facial landmarks, clothing attributes, and bounding boxes. It is intended for supervised training and benchmarking of person attribute recognition, fine‑grained clothing classification, pose estimation, and portrait editing or re‑identification models. Gentlemen supports evaluation of model robustness to variation in appearance and wardrobe and can be used to study bias and generalization in male‑focused visual tasks.

Common Voice 11.0 is a large-scale, crowdsourced multilingual speech corpus of short validated audio clips paired with text transcriptions and speaker metadata (age, gender, accent, vote counts). It covers many languages and accents, provides segmented WAV files with standard train/validation/test splits and accompanying TSV metadata, and emphasizes diversity and low-resource language coverage. Designed for training and evaluating ASR, TTS, language identification, speaker recognition, and related speech tasks, it supports development of robust, real-world speech models.

ArguAna-PL is a Polish-language argumentation dataset for evaluating embeddings on retrieval and stance/relevance tasks. It contains short claims or prompts paired with user comments and arguments annotated for relevance and stance (e.g., supporting, opposing, or neutral). The dataset is used in MTEB to benchmark embedding models for semantic similarity, argument retrieval, and stance/argument mining in Polish text.

MTEB DBPedia-PL is a Polish-language topic classification dataset derived from DBpedia, containing short text records labeled with topical categories. Included in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) as a default task, it is used to evaluate embedding models on semantic classification, clustering, and retrieval in Polish. The dataset tests models’ ability to capture topical and contextual distinctions in short, knowledge-base-derived texts.

FiQA-PL (default) is a financial-domain benchmark in MTEB containing short financial texts annotated with price-impact (price-loss) scores. It is designed to evaluate sentence and document embeddings on regression and ranking/semantic-similarity tasks in finance, measuring a model’s ability to capture market-relevant signals for forecasting, retrieval, and downstream financial analysis.

MTEB HotpotQA-PL is a passage-level retrieval benchmark derived from the HotpotQA multi-hop QA dataset. It pairs natural-language questions with their supporting paragraphs among distractors, enabling evaluation of embedding models on semantic retrieval, reranking, and multi-hop reasoning. Included in MTEB to measure embedding quality for retrieval-augmented QA tasks using standard train/validation/test splits.

MTEB MSMARCO-PL (default) is the passage-level MS MARCO subset used in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark to evaluate semantic retrieval and embedding quality. It contains real-world search queries paired with candidate passages and human relevance labels, enabling assessment of dense retrieval and semantic search models at scale. The dataset stresses robustness to noisy, short queries and is commonly used with ranking metrics (e.g., MRR@K, recall) to compare embedding and retrieval approaches.

MTEB NFCorpus-PL (default) is a Polish-language retrieval benchmark in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), designed to evaluate the quality of sentence and document embeddings for semantic search. It comprises Polish queries paired with candidate documents and relevance annotations, enabling assessment of embedding models on dense retrieval and semantic relevance tasks. The dataset covers diverse Polish text domains and is intended for benchmarking and comparing embedding methods on Polish semantic search scenarios.

MTEB NQ-PL (default) is a benchmark dataset within the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark for evaluating text embeddings on Polish question-to-passage retrieval. It provides Polish Natural Questions-style queries paired with relevant Wikipedia passages and standard train/validation/test splits with relevance labels. The dataset is intended for measuring embedding quality in semantic search, dense retrieval, and ranking tasks, and for assessing multilingual or language-specific embedding models on real-world question-answer retrieval scenarios.

Quora-PL (default) is a Polish paraphrase/semantic-similarity dataset derived from Quora question pairs, consisting of paired questions labeled as duplicates or non-duplicates. Included in MTEB to benchmark sentence embeddings, it is used for paraphrase identification, semantic retrieval, and clustering on short, question-style texts with standardized splits and evaluation metrics.

SCIDOCS-PL is a Polish-language scientific-document benchmark in the MTEB default suite designed to evaluate text embeddings for semantic search and retrieval in the scholarly domain. It contains Polish scientific documents paired with query-like inputs and graded relevance annotations, enabling assessment of dense retrieval, reranking, and semantic similarity performance. The dataset stresses domain-specific vocabulary and long-form content, making it useful for measuring embedding models’ ability to retrieve and rank relevant academic texts in Polish.

MTEB SciFact-PL (default) is a Polish-language scientific claim verification dataset adapted from SciFact, consisting of scientific claims paired with candidate evidence sentences extracted from scientific abstracts and annotated with stance labels (Supported, Refuted, Not Enough Info). It is designed to evaluate text embedding models on tasks such as evidence retrieval, claim classification, and semantic matching in the scientific domain for Polish. The dataset enables benchmarking of embedding quality for fact-checking and evidence-ranking workflows, measuring how well models capture claim–evidence relationships and domain-specific semantic nuance.

MTEB TRECCOVID-PL (default) is a benchmark dataset in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) that adapts the TREC-COVID retrieval collection for Polish. It provides COVID-19–related documents, queries, and relevance judgments to evaluate semantic search and retrieval performance of text embeddings and ranking models in a domain-specific, Polish-language biomedical setting.

AlloProfClusteringP2P is an MTEB benchmark dataset for evaluating text embeddings on clustering and pairwise (point-to-point) similarity tasks. It provides profile-like text items with pairwise annotations indicating whether two items belong to the same cluster, enabling assessment of embedding quality for clustering, pairwise retrieval, and link-prediction scenarios. The default (P2P) protocol evaluates models on pairwise similarity discrimination and downstream clustering performance using standard metrics such as pairwise precision/recall/F1 and clustering measures (ARI, NMI).

AlloProfClusteringS2S is an MTEB benchmark for evaluating sentence embedding models on clustering short textual profiles. It contains individual short texts grouped into semantic clusters and assesses how well embeddings separate and group semantically similar sentences. Models are evaluated using standard clustering metrics (e.g., ARI, NMI, F1) using the dataset’s default train/validation/test splits to enable consistent comparisons.

MTEB AlloprofReranking (default) is a reranking benchmark in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark suite built from French educational queries sourced from the Alloprof platform. Each example pairs a student query with an initial set of candidate passages/documents and graded relevance labels for supervised evaluation of reranking methods. It is intended to evaluate embedding-based reranking and semantic retrieval models for educational question answering and short-document retrieval in French using standard ranking metrics (e.g., MRR, nDCG).

MTEB AlloprofRetrieval is a retrieval benchmark derived from the Alloprof educational platform, containing student queries paired with relevant educational documents or passages and relevance annotations. It is designed to evaluate semantic search and dense retrieval models in the educational domain using MTEB’s default retrieval protocol. The collection helps assess embedding quality for ranking and retrieval tasks by measuring how well models retrieve accurate, pedagogically relevant resources for real student queries.

ArguAna (default) is an MTEB dataset for evaluating text embeddings on argumentative similarity and retrieval. It comprises argumentative texts from online debates with annotations indicating relatedness and stance between argument pairs, enabling assessment of how well embeddings capture semantic and argumentative relations. It is commonly used for retrieval, clustering, and similarity tasks to benchmark embedding models on argument mining and debate-oriented language.

ArxivClusteringP2P (default) is a clustering benchmark from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) built from arXiv papers (titles and abstracts) grouped by subject categories. It evaluates embedding models’ ability to group scientific documents into topical clusters and to recover paper-to-paper semantic relationships, supporting unsupervised clustering and cluster-quality metrics such as purity and NMI. The dataset is useful for benchmarking document embeddings on topic coherence and discovery in scientific literature.

ArxivClusteringS2S is a clustering benchmark derived from arXiv papers for evaluating text embedding and clustering methods in a sequence-to-sequence context.
