The dataset is suited for assessing translation quality, robustness, and generalization between English and Russian.

ntrex_ru-en is a Russian–English parallel corpus for machine translation and cross-lingual research. It provides sentence-level aligned pairs extracted from news and web sources to support supervised NMT training, evaluation, and domain adaptation. The dataset is commonly used as a benchmark for translation quality, domain robustness, and bilingual lexical induction.

Asian Language Treebank (ALT) is a multilingual treebank of several Asian languages, providing sentence-level corpora annotated with syntactic structure and part-of-speech tags. It supplies token-level morphosyntactic annotations and sentence alignments that support supervised training and evaluation of POS taggers, syntactic parsers, and cross-lingual transfer methods. ALT serves as a benchmark for research on multilingual syntactic analysis, typology-aware modeling, and improving NLP tools for Asian languages.

Various is a heterogeneous benchmark dataset that aggregates images and annotations from multiple sources and domains to provide diverse scenes, imaging conditions, and label distributions. It is designed to evaluate and train models for cross-domain generalization, domain adaptation, robustness to distribution shift, and multi-task learning across tasks such as classification, detection, segmentation, and restoration. By combining varied resolutions, scene types, and noise/artifact patterns, Various serves as a challenging real-world testbed for assessing model performance and generalizability.

Custom Hindi–Kangri Parallel Corpus is a sentence-aligned bilingual dataset pairing Hindi and Kangri texts for supervised cross-lingual learning. Curated and quality-checked across diverse domains (e.g., news, conversational, and cultural materials), it provides parallel sentence pairs and alignments to support machine translation, bilingual lexicon induction, word alignment, transfer learning, and evaluation of low-resource language models. The corpus is intended to facilitate research and development for Kangri, a low-resource Western Pahari language, by enabling training and assessment of translation and cross-lingual representation methods.

rahular/itihasa is a curated corpus of Itihāsa and related historical/epic narratives from South Asian tradition, provided for NLP research. The dataset contains long-form narrative passages (original-language text and available translations) cleaned and segmented for downstream tasks such as language modeling, summarization, question answering, retrieval, and style/domain adaptation. It is suitable for studying narrative structure, cultural knowledge grounding, and pre-modern text processing in multilingual pipelines.

UCF-Crime is a large-scale dataset for video anomaly detection collected from real-world surveillance (CCTV) footage. It contains roughly 1,900 long, untrimmed videos covering a wide variety of anomalous events (e.g., robbery, assault, accidents, vandalism) alongside normal activities, with annotations indicating anomalous segments. Designed to reflect realistic, long-duration surveillance scenarios, UCF-Crime is a challenging benchmark for developing and evaluating methods for anomaly detection and temporal localization, including supervised and weakly supervised approaches.

VDC is a dataset for video deblurring and temporal restoration, comprising real-world blurry video sequences paired with corresponding sharp frames captured across diverse scenes and motion patterns. It is designed to support supervised training and evaluation of temporally-aware deblurring models, promoting restoration of frame-level sharpness while preserving temporal consistency. VDC serves as a benchmark for measuring model performance and generalization in practical video restoration and downstream video analysis tasks.

TriviaQA is a large-scale text-based question answering dataset containing over 650,000 question-answer pairs with corresponding evidence documents from Wikipedia and the web. It is designed to be more challenging than traditional QA datasets, as answers may not be directly extractable as text spans and require reasoning over long and diverse contexts. The dataset includes both human-verified and automatically generated question-answer pairs, supporting research in complex reading comprehension and open-domain question answering tasks.

The **WebQuestions** dataset is a question answering dataset using Freebase as the knowledge base and contains 6,642 question-answer pairs. It was created by crawling questions through the Google Suggest API, and then obtaining answers using Amazon Mechanical Turk. The original split uses 3,778 examples for training and 2,032 for testing. All answers are defined as Freebase entities. OpenBookQA is a multiple-choice question-answering dataset designed to evaluate understanding of elementary-level science through open book exam-style questions. It contains nearly 6,000 questions that require applying a small set of core science facts to novel scenarios, supplemented by broad common knowledge beyond the core facts. The dataset includes training mappings from questions to the core facts they test, as well as crowd-sourced common knowledge facts. It is challenging for simple retrieval or word co-occurrence methods, encouraging development of reasoning and knowledge integration in AI systems.

DocVQA test is a visual question answering dataset designed to evaluate models' ability to understand and reason about image content in response to natural language questions. As a benchmark for vision-language models, it is used to assess performance in zero-shot and few-shot settings, particularly in tasks requiring grounding of answers to specific image regions. Models such as Qwen-VL and Qwen-VL-Chat have been evaluated on this dataset to demonstrate improvements in visual grounding, text-reading, and question answering accuracy. Large language models (LLMs), after being aligned with vision models and integrated into vision-language models (VLMs), can bring impressive improvement in image reasoning tasks. This was shown by the recently released GPT-4V(ison), LLaVA-1.5, etc. However, the strong language prior in these SOTA LVLMs can be a double-edged sword: they may ignore the image context and solely rely on the (even contradictory) language prior for reasoning. In contrast, the vision modules in VLMs are weaker than LLMs and may result in misleading visual representations, which are then translated to confident mistakes by LLMs. To study these two types of VLM mistakes, i.e., language hallucination and visual illusion, we curated HallusionBench, an image-context reasoning benchmark that is still challenging to even GPT-4V and LLaVA-1.5. We provide a detailed analysis of examples in HallusionBench, which sheds novel insights on the illusion or hallucination of VLMs and how to improve them in the future.

desc: MT-Bench is a multi-turn evaluation dataset for conversational and instruction-following language models. It contains curated dialogue prompts spanning diverse topics, reference responses, and human preference or quality annotations (pairwise comparisons and scalar ratings) to assess helpfulness, clarity, factuality and safety. Designed for reliable ranking and fine-grained analysis, MT-Bench supports both automated metrics and human-in-the-loop evaluation to benchmark model improvements in conversational competence and alignment.

TruthfulQA is a benchmark for evaluating language models’ truthfulness and tendency to hallucinate in zero-shot settings. It comprises several hundred human-authored, open-ended questions across diverse domains (science, history, health, etc.) that are adversarially designed to elicit false, misleading, or confidently fabricated answers. Models are evaluated without in-context examples or external access, with metrics that assess correct, truthful responses versus common misconceptions and hallucinations. TruthfulQA is used to compare model reliability, guide improvements in calibration and factuality, and study failure modes in open-ended generation.

MathQA is a benchmark dataset designed for math word problem solving, focusing on the task of translating natural language narratives into precise mathematical operations. It extends the AQuA dataset by providing fully specified operational programs that explicitly represent the solution steps, enabling models to perform both numerical and logical reasoning. The dataset consists of textual math problems that require understanding complex problem statements expressed in everyday language and converting them into executable mathematical expressions. MathQA challenges models to handle the dual aspects of symbolic reasoning and numerical computation, emphasizing the importance of capturing reusable numerical properties beyond mere number values. It supports research in developing advanced reasoning techniques and contextual number representation learning, as demonstrated by recent models evaluated on it. MathQA serves as a valuable resource for training and evaluating systems that integrate language understanding with mathematical problem-solving skills, facilitating progress in interpretable and accurate automated reasoning over math word problems.

PersianQA is a Persian-language question answering dataset for machine reading comprehension, containing human-annotated passages paired with questions and ground-truth answers. It is designed to train and evaluate QA models on Persian text, supporting extractive and generative approaches by providing answer spans or short text responses aligned to source passages. The dataset includes standardized splits for training, validation, and testing, making it useful for benchmarking model performance, studying cross-lingual transfer, and advancing Persian NLP research.

PopQA is an open-domain question answering dataset containing approximately 14,000 question-answer pairs. Each pair is annotated with fine-grained Wikidata entity identifiers, Wikipedia page view statistics, and relationship type information, enabling detailed entity-centric reasoning and analysis. The dataset supports research in knowledge-based question answering and entity linking tasks.

The dataset is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike License. Compared to the preprocessed version of Penn Treebank (PTB), WikiText-2 is over 2 times larger and WikiText-103 is over 110 times larger. The WikiText dataset also features a far larger vocabulary and retains the original case, punctuation and numbers - all of which are removed in PTB. As it is composed of full articles, the dataset is well suited for models that can take advantage of long term dependencies. Source: Image Source:

It has been widely used for benchmarking in image classification and object detection tasks, particularly through the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC). The dataset includes both image-level labels indicating the presence or absence of object classes and object-level annotations with bounding boxes around instances. Due to copyright restrictions, only image URLs and thumbnails are publicly available. ImageNet has significantly contributed to advancements in computer vision by providing a comprehensive and diverse set of labeled images for training and evaluation.

Charts are very popular for analyzing data. When exploring charts, people often ask a variety of complex reasoning questions that involve several logical and arithmetic operations. They also commonly refer to visual features of a chart in their questions. However, most existing datasets do not focus on such complex reasoning questions as their questions are template-based and answers come from a fixed-vocabulary. In this work, we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9.6K human-written questions as well as 23.1K questions generated from human-written chart summaries. To address the unique challenges in our benchmark involving visual and logical reasoning over charts, we present two transformer-based models that combine visual features and the data table of the chart in a unified way to answer questions. While our models achieve the state-of-the-art results on the previous datasets as well as on our benchmark, the evaluation also reveals several challenges in answering complex reasoning questions.

The MMLU-Pro dataset is an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark. It's designed to be more robust and challenging, aiming to rigorously benchmark large language models' capabilities in language comprehension and reasoning across diverse domains. Here are some key features of the MMLU-Pro dataset: - **Increased Complexity**: It includes more reasoning-focused questions and expands the choice set from four to ten options, reducing the likelihood of random guessing and increasing the evaluation's complexity¹. - **Elimination of Trivial Questions**: MMLU-Pro removes trivial and noisy questions found in the original MMLU, making it a more discriminative benchmark². - **Stability Under Varying Prompts**: The dataset shows greater stability under varying prompts, with a decreased sensitivity of model scores to prompt variations². - **Better Performance with Reasoning**: Models utilizing Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning achieved better performance on MMLU-Pro compared to direct answering². - **Size and Scope**: The dataset contains 12K complex questions across various disciplines¹⁴. **GPQA** stands for **Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark**. It's a challenging dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and scalable oversight mechanisms. Let me provide more details about it: - **Description**: GPQA consists of **448 multiple-choice questions** meticulously crafted by domain experts in **biology, physics, and chemistry**. These questions are intentionally designed to be **high-quality and extremely difficult**. - **Expert Accuracy**: Even experts who hold or are pursuing **PhDs in the corresponding domains** achieve only **65% accuracy** on these questions (or **74%** when excluding clear mistakes identified in retrospect). - **Google-Proof**: The questions are "Google-proof," meaning that even with **unrestricted access to the web**, highly skilled non-expert validators only reach an accuracy of **34%** despite spending over 30 minutes searching for answers. - **AI Systems Difficulty**: State-of-the-art AI systems, including our strongest **GPT-4 based baseline**, achieve only **39% accuracy** on this challenging dataset. The difficulty of GPQA for both skilled non-experts and cutting-edge AI systems makes it an excellent resource for conducting **realistic scalable oversight experiments**. These experiments aim to explore ways for human experts to reliably obtain truthful information from AI systems that surpass human capabilities¹³. In summary, GPQA serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the robustness and limitations of language models, especially when faced with complex and nuanced questions. Its difficulty level encourages research into effective oversight methods, bridging the gap between AI and human expertise. FLORES is a multilingual machine translation benchmark released by Facebook AI Research (notably FLORES-101) that provides curated, human-translated parallel sentences across a large set of languages—including many low-resource and typologically diverse languages. Its sentence-level dev and test splits (drawn and cleaned from sources like Wikipedia) are designed for robust evaluation of neural MT and cross-lingual models across many language pairs. FLORES is widely used to compare translation quality and generalization in multilingual systems and to drive research on low-resource and massively multilingual translation.

XQuAD is a multilingual extractive question-answering benchmark derived from SQuAD v1.1 by translating a subset of examples into multiple target languages. Each example contains a context paragraph, a question, and a span-level answer in the target language, enabling evaluation of cross-lingual transfer, zero-shot and fine-tuned QA models. XQuAD is commonly used to measure robustness to language shifts and to compare multilingual representations and transfer learning methods for reading comprehension.

XNLI (Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference) is a multilingual benchmark of premise–hypothesis sentence pairs labeled with entailment, contradiction, or neutral. It extends the English MultiNLI corpus via professional translations into multiple languages to enable evaluation of cross-lingual transfer, multilingual encoders, and zero-shot/fine-tuned NLI performance across languages.

ner is a dataset for named entity recognition containing tokenized sentences annotated with entity spans and classes (e.g., PERSON, LOCATION, ORGANIZATION, MISC). It provides supervised sequence-labeling examples (often in BIO/BILOU format) to train and evaluate models that detect and classify named entities in text. The dataset is intended for benchmarking NER systems and supports common evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, and F1; it is useful for developing information extraction, question answering, and other downstream NLP applications that rely on accurate entity identification.

STS is a semantic textual similarity dataset of sentence pairs annotated with continuous similarity scores (commonly 0–5) indicating degree of semantic equivalence. Collected from diverse sources (news, captions, forums) and provided with standard train/dev/test splits (e.g., SemEval STS tasks and STS Benchmark), it is used to train and evaluate sentence embeddings, paraphrase detection, semantic search, and regression models. Performance is typically measured by correlation with human judgments (Pearson/Spearman), making STS a standard benchmark for sentence-level semantic similarity.

CatalanQA is a Catalan-language question answering dataset of context–question–answer triplets designed for machine reading comprehension. It provides annotated passages with corresponding questions and extractive answer spans to enable supervised training and evaluation of QA models in Catalan. The dataset supports research on monolingual QA, cross-lingual transfer, and adaptation of pretrained multilingual or Catalan-specific language models to downstream comprehension tasks.

MS-COCO is a large-scale, multimodal dataset widely used for pose estimation, object detection, segmentation, and visual reasoning tasks. It contains over 330,000 images with rich annotations, including detailed human pose keypoints, object instances, attributes, and relationships. The dataset is particularly valuable for human-centric vision tasks due to its diverse and realistic scenes, with annotations capturing fine-grained human body configurations and spatial interactions. While it includes many untagged images and some data quality issues, its extensive scale and variety make it a foundational resource for training and evaluating vision models. Pose estimation on MS-COCO has been leveraged in models such as UniHCP and neuro-symbolic frameworks for human perception, where keypoint predictions are used to improve downstream tasks like human parsing, attribute prediction, and pedestrian detection. The Food-101 dataset contains 101 food categories with 750 training images and 250 test images per category, totaling approximately 101,000 images. The test labels have been manually verified for accuracy, while the training set may contain some label noise. This dataset is widely used for food image classification tasks in computer vision research.

COCO 2017 is a large-scale, multimodal dataset widely used for object detection, segmentation, and few-shot learning in computer vision. It contains approximately 330,000 images with annotations for 80 object categories, including bounding boxes, segmentation masks, and keypoints. The dataset is diverse, covering a broad range of real-world scenes and object appearances, making it ideal for training and evaluating object detection models under various conditions. Its use in few-shot detection is particularly valuable, as models pre-trained or fine-tuned on COCO demonstrate strong generalization when trained with limited labeled data. Recent advances, such as DETReg, leverage COCO for self-supervised pretraining of entire detection architectures—including localization and feature embedding—improving performance in low-data and few-shot regimes. The cats_vs_dogs dataset is a binary image classification dataset consisting of images of cats and dogs, commonly used for training and evaluating image classification models. It contains a balanced split of approximately 25,000 images per class, making it a foundational resource for introductory machine learning and computer vision education. The dataset is designed to test a model’s ability to distinguish between two distinct visual categories, emphasizing fundamental concepts such as feature extraction, model generalization, and accuracy in real-world image recognition. While small in scale compared to large-scale datasets, it provides a clear and accessible benchmark for evaluating model performance in a controlled setting. Due to its simplicity and well-defined task, it is frequently used in academic tutorials, model development pipelines, and as a baseline for comparing new algorithms. The dataset supports both traditional machine learning and deep learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks, and is widely adopted in educational

The Stanford Cars dataset contains 16,185 images of cars categorized into 196 classes based on make, model, and year. The images are divided nearly equally into training and testing sets, with approximately 8,144 training images and 8,041 testing images. Each image has a resolution of 360 by 240 pixels. The dataset is commonly used for fine-grained image classification tasks in computer vision.

The Digital Retinal Images for Vessel Extraction (DRIVE) dataset is designed for retinal vessel segmentation tasks. It contains 40 color fundus images, including several with abnormal pathology, collected from a diabetic retinopathy screening program in the Netherlands. Images were captured using a Canon CR5 non-mydriatic 3CCD camera with a 45-degree field of view, each with a resolution of 584 by 565 pixels and 8 bits per color channel. The dataset is split evenly into 20 training and 20 testing images. Each image includes a circular field of view mask. The training images have one manual vessel segmentation by an expert ophthalmologist, while the testing images have two manual segmentations from different observers, with the first observer's segmentation used as ground truth for evaluation.

desc: MM-Vet is a large-scale multimodal dataset designed to evaluate and advance integrated capabilities in visual question answering and related multimodal tasks. It encompasses diverse data samples that combine language, vision, and audio modalities, supporting complex reasoning across image content, natural language queries, and speech inputs. By including extensive multi-modal examples—such as images paired with questions and corresponding answers, along with long speech segments—MM-Vet facilitates the development and benchmarking of models capable of holistic understanding and interaction across multiple sensory inputs. The dataset addresses challenges in aligning and jointly reasoning over heterogeneous data types, promoting research in efficient and robust multimodal large language models. MM-Vet has been instrumental in evaluating state-of-the-art models that integrate vision, language, and audio, enabling advancements in tasks like visual question answering, speech comprehension, and cross-modal generation. Its scale and diversity make it a valuable resource for training and assessing models

MVBench is a comprehensive Multi-modal Video understanding Benchmark. It was introduced to evaluate the comprehension capabilities of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly their temporal understanding in dynamic video tasks. MVBench covers 20 challenging video tasks that cannot be effectively solved with a single frame. It introduces a novel static-to-dynamic method to define these temporal-related tasks. By transforming various static tasks into dynamic ones, it enables the systematic generation of video tasks that require a broad spectrum of temporal skills, ranging from perception to cognition.

MMLU (5-Shot) is a broad multi-task evaluation benchmark of multiple‑choice questions covering 57 academic and professional subjects (STEM, humanities, social sciences, etc.), drawn from exams and curricula to test factual knowledge and problem-solving. The 5‑shot variant evaluates few‑shot in‑context learning by providing five exemplar QA pairs per task during inference, measuring a model’s ability to generalize across diverse domains without task-specific fine‑tuning. It yields per-task and aggregate accuracy metrics, serving as a standard challenge for assessing large language models’ breadth of knowledge and reasoning in low‑shot conditions.

HellaSwag (10-Shot) is a few-shot variant of the HellaSwag commonsense reasoning benchmark that evaluates a model’s ability to choose the correct narrative continuation given a short context. Each example pairs a context with multiple-choice endings (one correct, several adversarial distractors crafted to be superficially plausible). The 10-shot setup provides ten labeled in-context examples for prompting or fine-tuning, making the task a focused measure of how well models generalize causal, physical, and commonsense reasoning from limited examples.

BBBP is a benchmark dataset in drug discovery used for evaluating machine learning models in predicting the blood-brain barrier permeability of small molecules. It consists of 28,000 chemical compounds with labeled outcomes indicating whether each compound can cross the blood-brain barrier. The dataset is widely used for graph-based modeling of molecular structures, where graph neural networks learn representations of molecular graphs to predict biological activity. Due to the scarcity of labeled data in drug discovery and the complexity of molecular interactions, BBBP serves as a key benchmark for assessing model generalization and performance under distributional shifts. Models are typically evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, ROC-AUC, and mean absolute error. The dataset highlights challenges in modeling chemical space and has been instrumental in advancing self-supervised pre-training strategies for graph neural networks, particularly in learning both local node and global graph-level representations. Its use in molecular property prediction

BACE is a multimodal dataset designed for drug discovery, focusing on molecular representation and property prediction. It includes structured molecular data, molecular images, and textual representations such as SMILES strings, enabling tasks like molecule generation, property classification, and image-to-text captioning. The dataset supports pretraining and fine-tuning of multi-modal models, including GIT-Mol and GTOT-Tuning, to align graph, image, and text modalities into a unified latent space. It contains over 200,000 molecular records across multiple downstream tasks, including classification of biological activity (e.g., BACE inhibition), toxicity, and solubility. The dataset addresses the challenge of sparse labels in molecular science by leveraging large-scale pretraining to transfer invariant knowledge from diverse modalities. Its structure supports both graph-based and vision-based modeling, making it valuable for developing models that can reason about molecular

The **Tox21** data set comprises 12,060 training samples and 647 test samples that represent chemical compounds. There are 801 "dense features" that represent chemical descriptors, such as molecular weight, solubility or surface area, and 272,776 "sparse features" that represent chemical substructures (ECFP10, DFS6, DFS8; stored in Matrix Market Format ). Machine learning methods can either use sparse or dense data or combine them. For each sample there are 12 binary labels that represent the outcome (active/inactive) of 12 different toxicological experiments. Note that the label matrix contains many missing values (NAs). GovReport is a dataset for long document summarization, with significantly longer documents and summaries. It consists of reports written by government research agencies including Congressional Research Service and U.S. Government Accountability Office. Compared with other long document summarization datasets, government report dataset has longer summaries and documents and requires reading in more context to cover salient words to be summarized.

mit_restaurant is a dataset of restaurant interior images annotated for visual scene understanding. Images are labeled with object-level annotations (e.g., tables, chairs, dishes, people, menus) and scene-layout cues to support tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and spatial layout estimation in dining environments. It is intended for training and evaluating computer vision models for robotics, service automation, and perception systems operating in restaurant-like settings.

AI2 ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge) is a benchmark of 7,787 genuine grade-school-level multiple-choice science questions designed to encourage research in advanced question answering. The dataset includes both an Easy Set and a Challenge Set, where the latter contains questions that were incorrectly answered by both retrieval-based and word co-occurrence algorithms. ARC also provides a corpus of over 14 million relevant science sentences and baseline neural models.

This is a subset on Hard split of the AI2 ARC benchmark with complex grade-school science questions.

## is a curated benchmark dataset for training and evaluating machine learning models. It provides annotated samples across diverse scenes and conditions to support tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation, with standardized train/validation/test splits and evaluation protocols. Designed to promote generalization and robustness, ## enables reproducible comparison of algorithms and development of practical, real-world ML systems.

MIRACL is a large-scale multilingual image–text retrieval dataset that pairs images with captions and translations across many languages. It is designed to train and evaluate cross-lingual and multilingual vision–language models for tasks such as image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval, image–caption matching, and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. MIRACL supports benchmarking of retrieval accuracy and representation alignment across languages and domains, enabling development of robust multilingual multimodal retrieval systems.

Rotten Tomatoes is a sentence-level sentiment dataset of short movie review snippets from the Rotten Tomatoes website, each labeled for binary sentiment (positive vs. negative). It is commonly used to train and evaluate supervised text-classification models, benchmark sentiment-analysis performance, and study transfer learning and domain adaptation for NLP systems.

MASSIVE is a parallel dataset of > 1M utterances across 51 languages with annotations for the Natural Language Understanding tasks of intent prediction and slot annotation. Utterances span 60 intents and include 55 slot types. MASSIVE was created by localizing the SLURP dataset, composed of general Intelligent Voice Assistant single-shot interactions.

Financial PhraseBank is a domain-specific sentiment analysis dataset focused on financial texts, designed to evaluate models' ability to classify the sentiment of financial phrases. Due to its domain focus, it serves as a critical benchmark for evaluating financial sentiment analysis models, particularly those fine-tuned on domain-specific pre-trained architectures like FinBERT. The dataset supports tasks such as sentiment classification and opinion mining, and is often used to assess model performance using standard metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and precision. Drop (3-Shot) is a few-shot variant of the DROP reading-comprehension benchmark, containing passages paired with questions that require discrete, multi-step numerical reasoning (counting, addition/subtraction, comparison, sorting) and span- or number-based answers. The dataset restricts supervision to three labeled examples per prompt/task to evaluate models' in-context learning and few-shot fine-tuning ability on challenging arithmetic and logical reasoning over text. It is intended to benchmark and stress-test NLP models' capability for compositional and numerical question answering under extreme data-scarcity.

HellaSwag is a large-scale commonsense natural language inference dataset designed to evaluate models' ability to understand everyday situations. It consists of multiple-choice questions where models must select the most plausible continuation of a given context. The dataset is challenging for state-of-the-art models but easy for humans, who achieve over 95% accuracy, making it a benchmark for commonsense reasoning in natural language processing.

WinoGrande is a large-scale dataset of 44k problems, inspired by the original WSC design, but adjusted to improve both the scale and the hardness of the dataset. The key steps of the dataset construction consist of (1) a carefully designed crowdsourcing procedure, followed by (2) systematic bias reduction using a novel AfLite algorithm that generalizes human-detectable word associations to machine-detectable embedding associations. Big-Bench-Hard (BBH) is a challenging benchmark dataset composed of 1,060 diverse, high-difficulty tasks designed to evaluate the reasoning and generalization capabilities of language models. It includes tasks that require complex reasoning, domain-specific knowledge, and multi-step problem-solving, making it a key benchmark for assessing zero-shot and few-shot learning performance. The dataset is used to evaluate how well language models—particularly smaller ones—can solve unseen, real-world problems without prior training on those tasks. In conjunction with the CoT Collection, which provides 1.84 million chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales across these tasks, BBH enables fine-tuning of models to improve step-by-step reasoning. Studies show that instruction-tuned models, such as Flan-T5, achieve significant gains in zero-shot accuracy—up to +4.34%

This dataset evaluates instruction following ability of large language models. There are 500+ prompts with instructions such as "write an article with more than 800 words", "wrap your response with double quotation marks", etc.

BoolQ is a large-scale yes/no question answering dataset consisting of naturally occurring questions paired with corresponding Wikipedia passages. Questions are derived from anonymized Google search queries identified as likely yes/no questions and are verified by human annotators for clarity and answerability. Annotators select relevant passages from Wikipedia articles and label each question with a yes or no answer based on the passage content. The dataset is designed to support research in machine reading comprehension and natural language understanding tasks involving binary question answering.

TriviaQA is a large-scale text-based question answering dataset containing over 650,000 question-answer pairs with corresponding evidence documents from Wikipedia and the web. It is designed to be more challenging than traditional QA datasets, as answers may not be directly extractable as text spans and require reasoning over long and diverse contexts. The dataset includes both human-verified and automatically generated question-answer pairs, supporting research in complex reading comprehension and open-domain question answering tasks.

ARC-C is a benchmark for compositional abstract reasoning built on the ARC-style paradigm of paired input–output grid transformation tasks. It contains diverse, few-shot examples that require inducing discrete rules and applying them to novel settings, stressing systematic generalization, compositionality, and algorithmic reasoning. ARC-C is intended to evaluate and compare neural, symbolic, and hybrid models on their ability to learn interpretable transformation programs from minimal supervision and to generalize across controlled variations of task structure.

The **SNLI** dataset (**Stanford Natural Language Inference**) consists of 570k sentence-pairs manually labeled as entailment, contradiction, and neutral. Premises are image captions from Flickr30k, while hypotheses were generated by crowd-sourced annotators who were shown a premise and asked to generate entailing, contradicting, and neutral sentences. Annotators were instructed to judge the relation between sentences given that they describe the same event. Each pair is labeled as “entailment”, “neutral”, “contradiction” or “-”, where “-” indicates that an agreement could not be reached. Source:

The **SciTail** dataset is an entailment dataset created from multiple-choice science exams and web sentences. Each question and the correct answer choice are converted into an assertive statement to form the hypothesis. We use information retrieval to obtain relevant text from a large text corpus of web sentences, and use these sentences as a premise P. We crowdsource the annotation of such premise-hypothesis pair as supports (entails) or not (neutral), in order to create the SciTail dataset. The dataset contains 27,026 examples with 10,101 examples with entails label and 16,925 examples with neutral label. Source: Image source:

MNLI (Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference) is a large-scale dataset for natural language inference containing approximately 433k sentence pairs (premise, hypothesis) annotated with three-way labels: entailment, contradiction, or neutral. Collected across multiple written and spoken genres, it enables training and evaluation of models that must generalize across diverse domains. MNLI includes matched and mismatched development/test sets to measure in-domain and cross-genre performance, making it a standard benchmark for sentence-level semantic understanding, transfer learning, and NLU model evaluation.

QQP (Quora Question Pairs) is a dataset of question pairs labeled as duplicate or non-duplicate, created to support paraphrase detection and semantic similarity research. It contains hundreds of thousands of question pairs collected from Quora with binary annotations, enabling supervised training and evaluation of classifiers, sentence embeddings, and retrieval models. QQP is commonly used as a benchmark for duplicate question detection, paraphrase identification, and related downstream NLP tasks.

The **QNLI** (**Question-answering NLI**) dataset is a Natural Language Inference dataset automatically derived from the Stanford Question Answering Dataset v1.1 (SQuAD). SQuAD v1.1 consists of question-paragraph pairs, where one of the sentences in the paragraph (drawn from Wikipedia) contains the answer to the corresponding question (written by an annotator). The dataset was converted into sentence pair classification by forming a pair between each question and each sentence in the corresponding context, and filtering out pairs with low lexical overlap between the question and the context sentence. The task is to determine whether the context sentence contains the answer to the question. This modified version of the original task removes the requirement that the model select the exact answer, but also removes the simplifying assumptions that the answer is always present in the input and that lexical overlap is a reliable cue. The QNLI dataset is part of GLUE benchmark. Source:

The Stanford Sentiment Treebank is a corpus with fully labeled parse trees that allows for a complete analysis of the compositional effects of sentiment in language. The corpus is based on the dataset introduced by Pang and Lee (2005) and consists of 11,855 single sentences extracted from movie reviews. It was parsed with the Stanford parser and includes a total of 215,154 unique phrases from those parse trees, each annotated by 3 human judges. Binary classification experiments on full sentences (negative or somewhat negative vs somewhat positive or positive with neutral sentences discarded) refer to the dataset as SST-2 or SST binary.

The Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA) is a dataset containing over 10,000 English sentences sourced from linguistics publications. Each sentence is annotated for linguistic acceptability, indicating whether it is grammatically acceptable or not, based on expert judgments. The dataset is split into training, development, and test sets, and is widely used for evaluating models on the task of acceptability classification in natural language processing.

Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC) is a corpus consists of 5,801 sentence pairs collected from newswire articles. Each pair is labelled if it is a paraphrase or not by human annotators. The whole set is divided into a training subset (4,076 sentence pairs of which 2,753 are paraphrases) and a test subset (1,725 pairs of which 1,147 are paraphrases). Source: Image Source:

The **Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE)** datasets come from a series of textual entailment challenges. Data from RTE1, RTE2, RTE3 and RTE5 is combined. Examples are constructed based on news and Wikipedia text.

ner is a dataset for named entity recognition containing tokenized sentences annotated with entity spans and classes (e.g., PERSON, LOCATION, ORGANIZATION, MISC). It provides supervised sequence-labeling examples (often in BIO/BILOU format) to train and evaluate models that detect and classify named entities in text. The dataset is intended for benchmarking NER systems and supports common evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, and F1; it is useful for developing information extraction, question answering, and other downstream NLP applications that rely on accurate entity identification.

TruthfulQA is a benchmark to measure whether a language model is truthful in generating answers to questions. The benchmark comprises 817 questions that span 38 categories, including health, law, finance and politics. The authors crafted questions that some humans would answer falsely due to a false belief or misconception. Image source:

desc: The MMLU-Pro dataset is an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark. It's designed to be more robust and challenging, aiming to rigorously benchmark large language models' capabilities in language comprehension and reasoning across diverse domains. Here are some key features of the MMLU-Pro dataset: - **Increased Complexity**: It includes more reasoning-focused questions and expands the choice set from four to ten options, reducing the likelihood of random guessing and increasing the evaluation's complexity¹. - **Elimination of Trivial Questions**: MMLU-Pro removes trivial and noisy questions found in the original MMLU, making it a more discriminative benchmark². - **Stability Under Varying Prompts**: The dataset shows greater stability under varying prompts, with a decreased sensitivity of model scores to prompt variations². - **Better Performance with Reasoning**: Models utilizing Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning achieved better performance on MMLU-Pro compared to direct answering². - **Size and Scope**: The dataset contains 12K complex questions across various disciplines¹⁴. MMLU (5-Shot) is a broad multi-task evaluation benchmark of multiple‑choice questions covering 57 academic and professional subjects (STEM, humanities, social sciences, etc.), drawn from exams and curricula to test factual knowledge and problem-solving. The 5‑shot variant evaluates few‑shot in‑context learning by providing five exemplar QA pairs per task during inference, measuring a model’s ability to generalize across diverse domains without task-specific fine‑tuning. It yields per-task and aggregate accuracy metrics, serving as a standard challenge for assessing large language models’ breadth of knowledge and reasoning in low‑shot conditions.

Winogrande (5-shot) is a large-scale, crowdsourced benchmark for commonsense pronoun resolution presented in a 5-shot few-shot evaluation setting. Each example asks a model to choose between two candidate antecedents for an ambiguous pronoun, requiring real-world and linguistic commonsense rather than surface cues. The 5-shot variant evaluates in-context or few-shot learners by providing five labeled exemplars before testing, making it useful for measuring few-shot generalization, robustness to spurious patterns, and comparative performance of foundation models on commonsense reasoning.

HellaSwag is a large-scale commonsense natural language inference dataset designed to evaluate models' ability to understand everyday situations. It consists of multiple-choice questions where models must select the most plausible continuation of a given context. The dataset is challenging for state-of-the-art models but easy for humans, who achieve over 95% accuracy, making it a benchmark for commonsense reasoning in natural language processing.

OpenBookQA is a multiple-choice question-answering dataset designed to evaluate understanding of elementary-level science through open book exam-style questions. It contains nearly 6,000 questions that require applying a small set of core science facts to novel scenarios, supplemented by broad common knowledge beyond the core facts. The dataset includes training mappings from questions to the core facts they test, as well as crowd-sourced common knowledge facts. It is challenging for simple retrieval or word co-occurrence methods, encouraging development of reasoning and knowledge integration in AI systems.

WinoGrande is a large-scale dataset of 44k problems, inspired by the original WSC design, but adjusted to improve both the scale and the hardness of the dataset. The key steps of the dataset construction consist of (1) a carefully designed crowdsourcing procedure, followed by (2) systematic bias reduction using a novel AfLite algorithm that generalizes human-detectable word associations to machine-detectable embedding associations. Drop (3-Shot) is a few-shot variant of the DROP reading-comprehension benchmark, containing passages paired with questions that require discrete, multi-step numerical reasoning (counting, addition/subtraction, comparison, sorting) and span- or number-based answers. The dataset restricts supervision to three labeled examples per prompt/task to evaluate models' in-context learning and few-shot fine-tuning ability on challenging arithmetic and logical reasoning over text. It is intended to benchmark and stress-test NLP models' capability for compositional and numerical question answering under extreme data-scarcity.

ARC (Easy) is a dataset designed for common sense reasoning tasks, consisting of 1,000 multiple-choice questions that require models to infer logical and everyday knowledge beyond pattern matching. The questions cover a range of real-world scenarios, such as social norms, physical interactions, and causal relationships, and are structured to assess a model’s ability to apply general world knowledge. The dataset is presented in natural language and is primarily used to evaluate and benchmark the reasoning capabilities of language models. While not as large or diverse as other datasets, ARC (Easy) provides a clear, accessible benchmark for assessing foundational reasoning skills in AI systems. Its focus on common sense makes it a key component in evaluating models’ understanding of human experience and context. Due to its well-defined structure and alignment with real-world reasoning, ARC (Easy) is widely used in research to test the effectiveness of pretraining and fine-tuning

The dataset was generated by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers in the following process (an example is provided in parentheses): 1. a crowd worker observes a source concept from ConceptNet (“River”) and three target concepts (“Waterfall”, “Bridge”, “Valley”) that are all related by the same ConceptNet relation (“AtLocation”), 2. the worker authors three questions, one per target concept, such that only that particular target concept is the answer, while the other two distractor concepts are not, (“Where on a river can you hold a cup upright to catch water on a sunny day?”, “Where can I stand on a river to see water falling without getting wet?”, “I’m crossing the river, my feet are wet but my body is dry, where am I?”) 3. for each question, another worker chooses one additional distractor from Concept Net (“pebble”, “stream”, “bank”), and the author another distractor (“mountain”, “bottom”, “island”) manually. BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) is a subset of the BIG-Bench evaluation suite, comprising 23 challenging tasks that current language models initially struggled to outperform compared to average human raters. These tasks require multi-step reasoning and highlight limitations of few-shot prompting without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) techniques. Applying CoT prompting significantly improves model performance, enabling models like PaLM and Codex to surpass average human-rater performance on many of these tasks. BBH serves as a benchmark to evaluate advanced reasoning capabilities in language models.

Each pair is annotated with fine-grained Wikidata entity identifiers, Wikipedia page view statistics, and relationship type information, enabling detailed entity-centric reasoning and analysis. The dataset supports research in knowledge-based question answering and entity linking tasks.

**GPQA** stands for **Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark**. It's a challenging dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and scalable oversight mechanisms. Let me provide more details about it: - **Description**: GPQA consists of **448 multiple-choice questions** meticulously crafted by domain experts in **biology, physics, and chemistry**. These questions are intentionally designed to be **high-quality and extremely difficult**. - **Expert Accuracy**: Even experts who hold or are pursuing **PhDs in the corresponding domains** achieve only **65% accuracy** on these questions (or **74%** when excluding clear mistakes identified in retrospect). - **Google-Proof**: The questions are "Google-proof," meaning that even with **unrestricted access to the web**, highly skilled non-expert validators only reach an accuracy of **34%** despite spending over 30 minutes searching for answers. - **AI Systems Difficulty**: State-of-the-art AI systems, including our strongest **GPT-4 based baseline**, achieve only **39% accuracy** on this challenging dataset. The difficulty of GPQA for both skilled non-experts and cutting-edge AI systems makes it an excellent resource for conducting **realistic scalable oversight experiments**. These experiments aim to explore ways for human experts to reliably obtain truthful information from AI systems that surpass human capabilities¹³. In summary, GPQA serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the robustness and limitations of language models, especially when faced with complex and nuanced questions. Its difficulty level encourages research into effective oversight methods, bridging the gap between AI and human expertise. MMLU measures a model’s ability to recall, reason, and apply knowledge across many disciplines, providing a standardized metric for cross-domain performance.

This dataset evaluates instruction following ability of large language models. There are 500+ prompts with instructions such as "write an article with more than 800 words", "wrap your response with double quotation marks", etc.

MATH500 is a benchmark dataset designed for evaluating mathematical reasoning abilities, focusing on challenging, PhD-level mathematics problems. It consists of a diverse set of problem-solving tasks that require multi-step reasoning, logical deduction, and deep mathematical knowledge. The dataset is part of a broader suite of reasoning benchmarks, including GPQA and AMC2023, and is used to assess the performance of large-scale reasoning models in complex mathematical domains. Problems span various subfields of mathematics and are structured to test both procedural knowledge and abstract reasoning. Due to the high cognitive demand and variability in problem complexity, MATH500 serves as a critical benchmark for evaluating the robustness, accuracy, and generalization capabilities of reasoning models. Its use in model evaluation highlights challenges such as knowledge insufficiency and error propagation in long-chain reasoning. MATH500 enables researchers to compare model performance across different architectures

Big-Bench-Hard (BBH) is a challenging benchmark dataset composed of 1,060 diverse, high-difficulty tasks designed to evaluate the reasoning and generalization capabilities of language models. It includes tasks that require complex reasoning, domain-specific knowledge, and multi-step problem-solving, making it a key benchmark for assessing zero-shot and few-shot learning performance. The dataset is used to evaluate how well language models—particularly smaller ones—can solve unseen, real-world problems without prior training on those tasks. In conjunction with the CoT Collection, which provides 1.84 million chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales across these tasks, BBH enables fine-tuning of models to improve step-by-step reasoning. Studies show that instruction-tuned models, such as Flan-T5, achieve significant gains in zero-shot accuracy—up to +4.34%

CoQA is a large-scale dataset designed for building conversational question answering systems. It contains over 127,000 questions and answers collected from more than 8,000 conversations, where two crowdworkers interact about a given passage. The dataset features conversational questions, free-form text answers, and evidence spans highlighted within passages. Passages are drawn from seven diverse domains, presenting challenges such as coreference resolution and pragmatic reasoning. CoQA aims to evaluate a machine's ability to understand text and answer interconnected questions in a conversational context.

Each example pairs a context with multiple-choice endings (one correct, several adversarial distractors crafted to be superficially plausible). The 10-shot setup provides ten labeled in-context examples for prompting or fine-tuning, making the task a focused measure of how well models generalize causal, physical, and commonsense reasoning from limited examples.

MathQA is a benchmark dataset designed for math word problem solving, focusing on the task of translating natural language narratives into precise mathematical operations. It extends the AQuA dataset by providing fully specified operational programs that explicitly represent the solution steps, enabling models to perform both numerical and logical reasoning. The dataset consists of textual math problems that require understanding complex problem statements expressed in everyday language and converting them into executable mathematical expressions. MathQA challenges models to handle the dual aspects of symbolic reasoning and numerical computation, emphasizing the importance of capturing reusable numerical properties beyond mere number values. It supports research in developing advanced reasoning techniques and contextual number representation learning, as demonstrated by recent models evaluated on it. MathQA serves as a valuable resource for training and evaluating systems that integrate language understanding with mathematical problem-solving skills, facilitating progress in interpretable and accurate automated reasoning over math word problems.

Some examples have no answer, indicated by empty long and short answer annotations. In some cases, the long answer is present but no short answer spans are identified. Additionally, a small portion of examples contain yes/no answers instead of span-based answers. This dataset is widely used for training and evaluating machine reading comprehension and open-domain question answering systems.

ARC-C is a benchmark for compositional abstract reasoning built on the ARC-style paradigm of paired input–output grid transformation tasks. It contains diverse, few-shot examples that require inducing discrete rules and applying them to novel settings, stressing systematic generalization, compositionality, and algorithmic reasoning. ARC-C is intended to evaluate and compare neural, symbolic, and hybrid models on their ability to learn interpretable transformation programs from minimal supervision and to generalize across controlled variations of task structure.

Big-Bench-Hard (BBH) is a challenging benchmark dataset composed of 1,060 diverse, high-difficulty tasks designed to evaluate the reasoning and generalization capabilities of language models. It includes tasks that require complex reasoning, domain-specific knowledge, and multi-step problem-solving, making it a key benchmark for assessing zero-shot and few-shot learning performance. The dataset is used to evaluate how well language models—particularly smaller ones—can solve unseen, real-world problems without prior training on those tasks. In conjunction with the CoT Collection, which provides 1.84 million chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales across these tasks, BBH enables fine-tuning of models to improve step-by-step reasoning. Studies show that instruction-tuned models, such as Flan-T5, achieve significant gains in zero-shot accuracy—up to +4.34%

**GPQA** stands for **Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark**. It's a challenging dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and scalable oversight mechanisms. Let me provide more details about it: - **Description**: GPQA consists of **448 multiple-choice questions** meticulously crafted by domain experts in **biology, physics, and chemistry**. These questions are intentionally designed to be **high-quality and extremely difficult**. - **Expert Accuracy**: Even experts who hold or are pursuing **PhDs in the corresponding domains** achieve only **65% accuracy** on these questions (or **74%** when excluding clear mistakes identified in retrospect). - **Google-Proof**: The questions are "Google-proof," meaning that even with **unrestricted access to the web**, highly skilled non-expert validators only reach an accuracy of **34%** despite spending over 30 minutes searching for answers. - **AI Systems Difficulty**: State-of-the-art AI systems, including our strongest **GPT-4 based baseline**, achieve only **39% accuracy** on this challenging dataset. The difficulty of GPQA for both skilled non-experts and cutting-edge AI systems makes it an excellent resource for conducting **realistic scalable oversight experiments**. These experiments aim to explore ways for human experts to reliably obtain truthful information from AI systems that surpass human capabilities¹³. In summary, GPQA serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the robustness and limitations of language models, especially when faced with complex and nuanced questions. Its difficulty level encourages research into effective oversight methods, bridging the gap between AI and human expertise. desc: **MMBench** is a multi-modality benchmark. It methodically develops a comprehensive evaluation pipeline, primarily comprised of two elements. The first element is a meticulously curated dataset that surpasses existing similar benchmarks in terms of the number and variety of evaluation questions and abilities. The second element introduces a novel CircularEval strategy and incorporates the use of ChatGPT. This implementation is designed to convert free-form predictions into pre-defined choices, thereby facilitating a more robust evaluation of the model's predictions.

Charts are very popular for analyzing data. When exploring charts, people often ask a variety of complex reasoning questions that involve several logical and arithmetic operations. They also commonly refer to visual features of a chart in their questions. However, most existing datasets do not focus on such complex reasoning questions as their questions are template-based and answers come from a fixed-vocabulary. In this work, we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9.6K human-written questions as well as 23.1K questions generated from human-written chart summaries. To address the unique challenges in our benchmark involving visual and logical reasoning over charts, we present two transformer-based models that combine visual features and the data table of the chart in a unified way to answer questions. While our models achieve the state-of-the-art results on the previous datasets as well as on our benchmark, the evaluation also reveals several challenges in answering complex reasoning questions.

The Natural Questions dataset is a large-scale question answering benchmark consisting of real anonymized Google search queries paired with corresponding Wikipedia pages. Each example includes a question, a long answer which is a passage from the Wikipedia page that answers the question, and one or more short answer spans extracted from the long answer. Some examples have no answer, indicated by empty long and short answer annotations. In some cases, the long answer is present but no short answer spans are identified. Additionally, a small portion of examples contain yes/no answers instead of span-based answers. This dataset is widely used for training and evaluating machine reading comprehension and open-domain question answering systems.

The dataset is known for its challenging question types, including those requiring spatial reasoning, object recognition, and commonsense understanding, which test both visual and linguistic comprehension. While it is a validation subset of the larger VQA v2 dataset, it is often used to benchmark performance and evaluate the effectiveness of vision-language models, particularly in few-shot learning and instruction tuning. The MMLU-Pro dataset is an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark. It's designed to be more robust and challenging, aiming to rigorously benchmark large language models' capabilities in language comprehension and reasoning across diverse domains. Here are some key features of the MMLU-Pro dataset: - **Increased Complexity**: It includes more reasoning-focused questions and expands the choice set from four to ten options, reducing the likelihood of random guessing and increasing the evaluation's complexity¹. - **Elimination of Trivial Questions**: MMLU-Pro removes trivial and noisy questions found in the original MMLU, making it a more discriminative benchmark². - **Stability Under Varying Prompts**: The dataset shows greater stability under varying prompts, with a decreased sensitivity of model scores to prompt variations². - **Better Performance with Reasoning**: Models utilizing Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning achieved better performance on MMLU-Pro compared to direct answering². - **Size and Scope**: The dataset contains 12K complex questions across various disciplines¹⁴. The **LAMBADA** (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) benchmark is an open-ended cloze task which consists of about 10,000 passages from BooksCorpus where a missing target word is predicted in the last sentence of each passage. The missing word is constrained to always be the last word of the last sentence and there are no candidate words to choose from. Examples were filtered by humans to ensure they were possible to guess given the context, i.e., the sentences in the passage leading up to the last sentence. Examples were further filtered to ensure that missing words could not be guessed without the context, ensuring that models attempting the dataset would need to reason over the entire paragraph to answer questions. MMLU (5-Shot) is a broad multi-task evaluation benchmark of multiple‑choice questions covering 57 academic and professional subjects (STEM, humanities, social sciences, etc.), drawn from exams and curricula to test factual knowledge and problem-solving. The 5‑shot variant evaluates few‑shot in‑context learning by providing five exemplar QA pairs per task during inference, measuring a model’s ability to generalize across diverse domains without task-specific fine‑tuning. It yields per-task and aggregate accuracy metrics, serving as a standard challenge for assessing large language models’ breadth of knowledge and reasoning in low‑shot conditions.

Winogrande (5-shot) is a large-scale, crowdsourced benchmark for commonsense pronoun resolution presented in a 5-shot few-shot evaluation setting. Each example asks a model to choose between two candidate antecedents for an ambiguous pronoun, requiring real-world and linguistic commonsense rather than surface cues. The 5-shot variant evaluates in-context or few-shot learners by providing five labeled exemplars before testing, making it useful for measuring few-shot generalization, robustness to spurious patterns, and comparative performance of foundation models on commonsense reasoning.

BBH (3-Shot) is a few-shot classification benchmark designed to evaluate models’ ability to learn novel categories from three labeled examples per class. The dataset is organized into episodic tasks: each episode provides a 3-shot support set and a query set sampled from a diverse set of classes, with standard train/validation/test splits for held-out class evaluation. BBH (3-Shot) is intended for meta-learning, transfer learning, and metric-learning research and is typically evaluated by average classification accuracy across many episodes under the prescribed protocol.

The Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA) dataset is designed to evaluate commonsense causal reasoning in natural language processing. It contains 1000 multiple-choice questions, divided equally into development and test sets. Each question presents a premise and two alternative sentences, and the task is to select the alternative that is more plausibly causally related to the premise. The correct answer is randomized to ensure a 50% chance baseline for random guessing. COPA is widely used to benchmark models' ability to understand and reason about cause-effect relationships in open-domain contexts.

HellaSwag is a large-scale commonsense natural language inference dataset designed to evaluate models' ability to understand everyday situations. It consists of multiple-choice questions where models must select the most plausible continuation of a given context. The dataset is challenging for state-of-the-art models but easy for humans, who achieve over 95% accuracy, making it a benchmark for commonsense reasoning in natural language processing.

The MMLU-Pro dataset is an enhanced version of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark. It's designed to be more robust and challenging, aiming to rigorously benchmark large language models' capabilities in language comprehension and reasoning across diverse domains. Here are some key features of the MMLU-Pro dataset: - **Increased Complexity**: It includes more reasoning-focused questions and expands the choice set from four to ten options, reducing the likelihood of random guessing and increasing the evaluation's complexity¹. - **Elimination of Trivial Questions**: MMLU-Pro removes trivial and noisy questions found in the original MMLU, making it a more discriminative benchmark². - **Stability Under Varying Prompts**: The dataset shows greater stability under varying prompts, with a decreased sensitivity of model scores to prompt variations². - **Better Performance with Reasoning**: Models utilizing Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning achieved better performance on MMLU-Pro compared to direct answering². - **Size and Scope**: The dataset contains 12K complex questions across various disciplines¹⁴. MATH500 is a benchmark dataset designed for evaluating mathematical reasoning abilities, focusing on challenging, PhD-level mathematics problems. It consists of a diverse set of problem-solving tasks that require multi-step reasoning, logical deduction, and deep mathematical knowledge. The dataset is part of a broader suite of reasoning benchmarks, including GPQA and AMC2023, and is used to assess the performance of large-scale reasoning models in complex mathematical domains. Problems span various subfields of mathematics and are structured to test both procedural knowledge and abstract reasoning. Due to the high cognitive demand and variability in problem complexity, MATH500 serves as a critical benchmark for evaluating the robustness, accuracy, and generalization capabilities of reasoning models. Its use in model evaluation highlights challenges such as knowledge insufficiency and error propagation in long-chain reasoning. MATH500 enables researchers to compare model performance across different architectures

PopQA is an open-domain question answering dataset containing approximately 14,000 question-answer pairs. Each pair is annotated with fine-grained Wikidata entity identifiers, Wikipedia page view statistics, and relationship type information, enabling detailed entity-centric reasoning and analysis. The dataset supports research in knowledge-based question answering and entity linking tasks.

**GPQA** stands for **Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark**. It's a challenging dataset designed to evaluate the capabilities of **Large Language Models (LLMs)** and scalable oversight mechanisms. Let me provide more details about it: - **Description**: GPQA consists of **448 multiple-choice questions** meticulously crafted by domain experts in **biology, physics, and chemistry**. These questions are intentionally designed to be **high-quality and extremely difficult**. - **Expert Accuracy**: Even experts who hold or are pursuing **PhDs in the corresponding domains** achieve only **65% accuracy** on these questions (or **74%** when excluding clear mistakes identified in retrospect). - **Google-Proof**: The questions are "Google-proof," meaning that even with **unrestricted access to the web**, highly skilled non-expert validators only reach an accuracy of **34%** despite spending over 30 minutes searching for answers. - **AI Systems Difficulty**: State-of-the-art AI systems, including our strongest **GPT-4 based baseline**, achieve only **39% accuracy** on this challenging dataset. The difficulty of GPQA for both skilled non-experts and cutting-edge AI systems makes it an excellent resource for conducting **realistic scalable oversight experiments**. These experiments aim to explore ways for human experts to reliably obtain truthful information from AI systems that surpass human capabilities¹³. In summary, GPQA serves as a valuable benchmark for assessing the robustness and limitations of language models, especially when faced with complex and nuanced questions. Its difficulty level encourages research into effective oversight methods, bridging the gap between AI and human expertise. ARC (Easy) is a dataset designed for common sense reasoning tasks, consisting of 1,000 multiple-choice questions that require models to infer logical and everyday knowledge beyond pattern matching. The questions cover a range of real-world scenarios, such as social norms, physical interactions, and causal relationships, and are structured to assess a model’s ability to apply general world knowledge. The dataset is presented in natural language and is primarily used to evaluate and benchmark the reasoning capabilities of language models. While not as large or diverse as other datasets, ARC (Easy) provides a clear, accessible benchmark for assessing foundational reasoning skills in AI systems. Its focus on common sense makes it a key component in evaluating models’ understanding of human experience and context. Due to its well-defined structure and alignment with real-world reasoning, ARC (Easy) is widely used in research to test the effectiveness of pretraining and fine-tuning

ANLI (Adversarial Natural Language Inference) is a large-scale NLI benchmark of sentence pairs labeled entailment, contradiction, or neutral, created via an iterative human-and-model-in-the-loop process. Crowdworkers were asked to write examples that fooled contemporary models across three rounds (R1–R3), producing challenging, adversarial instances that expose model weaknesses. ANLI is used to evaluate robustness, adversarial generalization, and out-of-distribution performance of NLI systems.

Big-Bench-Hard (BBH) is a challenging benchmark dataset composed of 1,060 diverse, high-difficulty tasks designed to evaluate the reasoning and generalization capabilities of language models. It includes tasks that require complex reasoning, domain-specific knowledge, and multi-step problem-solving, making it a key benchmark for assessing zero-shot and few-shot learning performance. The dataset is used to evaluate how well language models—particularly smaller ones—can solve unseen, real-world problems without prior training on those tasks. In conjunction with the CoT Collection, which provides 1.84 million chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales across these tasks, BBH enables fine-tuning of models to improve step-by-step reasoning. Studies show that instruction-tuned models, such as Flan-T5, achieve significant gains in zero-shot accuracy—up to +4.34%
